signal.desc: Descriptor index src0 was resolved from, for the unit to return in the completion token's src0 field; valid when src0_id_v is set.

signal.name: src0_id_v
signal.desc: src0 operand is present. Distinguishes 'reads descriptor 0' from 'reads nothing', which the id alone cannot -- the same reason Table 4.2.8 carries valid bits.

signal.name: src1_id
signal.desc: Descriptor index src1 was resolved from; valid when src1_id_v is set.

signal.name: src1_id_v
signal.desc: src1 operand is present. Clear for a one-operand instruction, which is every XPU dispatch.

signal.name: dst_id
signal.desc: Descriptor index dst was resolved from, for the unit to return in the completion token's dst field; valid when dst_id_v is set.

signal.name: dst_id_v
signal.desc: Destination is present. Clear for an instruction that writes no descriptor, whose completion therefore sets no Rdy bit.

signal.name: op
signal.desc: Instruction opcode. Only OVMM, VCALL and XPU are dispatched on this port.

signal.name: src0
signal.desc: Operand-0 source descriptor, resolved from the instruction's src0 descriptor index.

signal.name: src1
signal.desc: Operand-1 source descriptor, resolved from the instruction's src1 descriptor index; all-zero when unused.

signal.name: dst
signal.desc: Destination descriptor, resolved from the instruction's dst descriptor index.

signal.name: vpu_kernel_addr
signal.desc: VPU kernel entry point: the VCALL instruction's pc_addr (29-bit HBM address field) resolved to a 64-bit byte address. Zero for OVMM/XPU.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Command valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Command ready (asserted by the execution unit).

ssot_gap.desc: Does this wire carry RESOLVED descriptors or descriptor INDICES? This spec says resolved: src0/src1/dst are full 64-byte descriptors, so the DFE reads the descriptor table and the execution unit never sees a handle. The DFE model's dispatch fifo disagrees -- it forwards the undecoded 64-bit instruction, i.e. indices -- which places descriptor resolution on the opposite side of the boundary. Both cannot be right, and a DFE model cannot be co-simulated against an RTL execution unit until one is chosen.
ssot_gap.assumed: This spec's reading: the DFE resolves. Chapter 4 §4.2.5.1 has the DFE resolve src0/src1 against the descriptor table and dispatch the resolved geometry, and a 3 x 512-bit payload is only justified if it carries descriptors.

ssot_gap.desc: How does an execution unit report a fault? The cmd channel has no response path beyond `ready`, and the completion interface carries no status field, so a decode fault, an address fault, or a numeric exception inside OVMM/VPU/XPU has nowhere to go.
ssot_gap.assumed: Faults do not occur; the model surfaces them through elog and a counter instead of over the interface.

hbm.name: hbm
hbm.desc: Tagged split-transaction HBM4E stack access port, per stack. Address and data are separate channels (AXI-style ar/r/aw/w/b); a multi-byte transfer is a burst of fixed-width beats with `last` on the final one, and every access names the stack it is addressed to.
hbm.notes: Split transaction: a request carries a tag, the completion returns it. Ordering is per-tag, not global. `w` has no tag (as in AXI4), so write beats follow `aw` in issue order and two outstanding writes may not interleave their data. `stack` is echoed on `r` and `b` for convenience only; `tag` is the only sound pairing. Address is stack-local: nothing on this port renumbers, decodes or stripes an address across stacks.

parameter.name: STACKS
parameter.desc: Number of HBM4E stacks reachable through this port: 0..2 north, 3..5 south. Six of them, kept as a parameter because it is the thing STACK_WIDTH is derived from and the thing an initiator range-checks against. Not a bit width -- a count.

parameter.name: STACK_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Stack selector. Six stacks is 3 bits. Values 6 and 7 are encodable and illegal; a target reports them as `stack_out_of_range` rather than aliasing them. Note the encoding is FLAT (0..5 with the side implied by the value), whereas RFC-T100-0005 §3 carries placement in a PTE as separate `stack[2:0]` and `side` fields -- one concept, two encodings, and this port uses the flat one.

parameter.name: ADDR_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Stack-local byte address. RFC-T100-0005 §1 pins the HBM byte offset of the tagged pointer at bits [41:0] -- a 42-bit / 4 TiB architectural envelope, chosen there specifically to absorb HBM4E growth with no ISA churn -- so 42 is the widest address the architecture admits and no wider field is justified. It is an upper bound, not a per-stack capacity claim: today a stack is 64 GiB (384 GiB / 6, RFC §1), so only the low 36 bits are populated. Sizing the port at 36 would encode today's capacity into every bundle layout and require a width change on the first growth the RFC says it wants to absorb silently.

parameter.name: LEN_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Transfer length in BYTES, not beats -- see the burst-geometry ssot_gap. 32 bits: unlike `stack`, nothing in the architecture bounds a single HBM burst, so there is no smaller number to derive and narrowing it would be inventing a limit. 32 bits is far more than any real transfer needs (RFC-T100-0005 §3 makes 4 KB the placement quantum) and costs 32 bits on two address channels; the alternative is a bound nobody has stated.

parameter.name: DATA_WIDTH
parameter.desc: One beat. THIS NUMBER IS A CHOICE, NOT ARCHITECTURE -- see the beat-width ssot_gap. It matches the TM port (ssot/interfaces/tm_interface.toml), which in turn matches the high-speed NoC beat, so the dominant traffic on this port -- a TDMA moving a tensor between HBM and TM -- does not need a width converter at either end. The DRAM-side numbers RFC-T100-0005 §3 gives are smaller and are quanta of the controller's internal decomposition, not of this port (~64 B per pseudo-channel, ~2 x 32 B BL8 bursts, 4 KB page as the stripe quantum), and the RFC states outright that the exact decomposition is pinned against final HBM4E JEDEC geometry, which does not exist yet. 1024 bits = 128 B is a whole multiple of the 32 B burst granule, so the choice does not conflict with those numbers; it is not derived from them either.

parameter.name: STRB_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Byte enables for one write beat, one bit per byte (DATA_WIDTH / 8). Its own parameter because the generator cannot yet evaluate an expression over another parameter; it must track DATA_WIDTH.

parameter.name: TAG_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Request tag, echoed on the completion. 32 bits -- wide enough that an initiator never has to reuse a tag while a request is outstanding, which is what per-tag ordering requires.

parameter.name: INITIATOR_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Initiator unit id, for ELOG attribution. Four bits match the TM port and allow every current HBM initiator, including NIC DMA, to have a distinct value. The id space is not yet canonical, so this interface fixes the width but does not invent an encoding.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Interface clock. All signals sampled on the rising edge.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset.

enum.name: HbmStatus
enum.desc: How an HBM access ended. Shared by the read-data and write-response channels.

member.name: ok
member.desc: Access completed normally.

member.name: stack_out_of_range
member.desc: `stack` is not in 0..5.

member.name: addr_out_of_range
member.desc: `addr` (or the span) is past the end of the stack.

member.name: ecc_uncorrectable
member.desc: ECC detected an error it could not correct; `data` is not trustworthy.

ar.desc: Read request: which stack, where in it, how many bytes, and who is asking.

signal.name: stack
signal.desc: Stack to read (0..5; 0-2 north, 3-5 south). The initiator names it; this port never derives it from the address.

signal.name: addr
signal.desc: Stack-local byte address of the first byte. Local to the stack named above: the same value on two different stacks is two different bytes.

signal.name: len
signal.desc: Bytes to read. 0 is not a legal request. Whether a burst may cross a 4 KB frame boundary is unsettled -- see the burst-geometry ssot_gap.

signal.name: tag
signal.desc: Echoed on every beat of the matching `r` burst. The only sound pairing between a request and its data, since ordering is per-tag.

signal.name: initiator
signal.desc: Unit id of the requester, for ELOG attribution and (later) per-initiator bandwidth accounting.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Read request valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Controller accepts the read request.

r.desc: One beat of read data, tagged, with a per-beat status and an end-of-burst marker.

signal.name: data
signal.desc: One beat of read data. On the final beat of a burst whose `len` is not a whole multiple of the beat, the bytes beyond `len` are undefined -- there is no read strobe to mask them.

signal.name: tag
signal.desc: The `tag` of the `ar` this beat belongs to. Every beat of a burst carries it.

signal.name: stack
signal.desc: The stack the data came from. Redundant with `tag`; do not pair on it.

signal.name: status
signal.desc: Outcome for THIS beat (like AXI's RRESP). Four bits for four codes, leaving room to add one -- an ECC CORRECTED code is the obvious candidate, since RFC-T100-0005 §4 has controller-generated ECC and only the uncorrectable case is reportable here -- without moving the bundle.

signal.name: last
signal.desc: Final beat of this burst. The consumer counts beats against it; nothing else on the channel says how long the burst is.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Read data valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Initiator accepts the beat.

aw.desc: Write request: which stack, where in it, how many bytes, and who is writing.

signal.name: stack
signal.desc: Stack to write (0..5; 0-2 north, 3-5 south).

signal.name: addr
signal.desc: Stack-local byte address of the first byte.

signal.name: len
signal.desc: Bytes to write. 0 is not a legal request. Must agree with the number of `w` beats and their strobes; a disagreement is a protocol error the port cannot report, since HbmStatus has no code for one.

signal.name: tag
signal.desc: Echoed on `b`. Required: a DMA cannot signal until the controller has the data, and the acknowledgement is what tells it so.

signal.name: initiator
signal.desc: Unit id of the writer, for ELOG attribution.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Write request valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Controller accepts the write request.

w.desc: One beat of write data with byte strobes and an end-of-burst marker. Untagged: beats follow `aw` in issue order.

signal.name: data
signal.desc: One beat of write data. Bytes whose strobe is 0 are not written and their value is ignored.

signal.name: strobe
signal.desc: Byte enables for `data`, one bit per byte. This is how a transfer that is not a whole number of beats terminates: the final beat masks the bytes past `len`. All ones is a full-width beat. Note that a partial write below the ECC codeword forces a read-modify-write in the controller (RFC-T100-0005 §4 stores ECC in a separate partition over a 256 B codeword); that cost is the controller's, not the port's, but a strobe is what makes it possible.

signal.name: last
signal.desc: Final beat of this write burst. The target may not raise `b` before it.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Write data valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Controller accepts the beat.

b.desc: Write completion: one acknowledgement per accepted `aw`, raised no earlier than the beat carrying `w.last`.

signal.name: tag
signal.desc: The `tag` of the `aw` being completed.

signal.name: stack
signal.desc: The stack written. Redundant with `tag`.

signal.name: status
signal.desc: Outcome for the whole write. Same encoding as `r.status` -- one HbmStatus means the same thing on both sides of the port by construction.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Write response valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Initiator accepts the response.

ssot_gap.desc: Who decides which stack a byte lands in? Three documents answer differently and this port has to pick one. (1) This port says the address is stack-local and interleaving across stacks is the INITIATOR's decision -- a DMA that wants to stripe issues one request per stack. (2) RFC-T100-0005 §3 says placement is the ALLOCATOR's: the PTE carries `stack[2:0]` and `side`, assigned at PTE-fill time, and the RFC is emphatic that there is no `mod 3` at access time and that mod-3 survives only as a software load-balancing heuristic. (3) The TM gap G11 records that pg ch 13 §13.1.1 does specify an HBM side -- interleaved 8 bytes at a time across TEs, with equations -- which is a fine-grained hardware interleave and is the thing the RFC rejected. Those cannot all be true of one machine: either a stack id is a field an initiator computes, a field the page table supplies, or nothing on the wire at all because the controller decodes a flat address. The port shape depends on the answer -- if it is the third, `stack` should not be a signal here.
ssot_gap.assumed: `addr` is stack-local, `stack` is an initiator-driven field, and this port neither decodes nor stripes. An initiator that wants to spread a tensor issues one transfer per stack and is responsible for the split; the model performs no interleave of its own. Where a stack id comes from upstream (page table, allocator policy, or a compile-time decision) is left to the initiator, so no policy is compiled in here.

ssot_gap.desc: How wide is one beat on this port? Nothing pins it. RFC-T100-0005 §3 gives DRAM-side quanta -- a 4 KB page as the stripe quantum, ~64 B per pseudo-channel, ~2 x 32 B BL8 bursts -- and then says outright that the exact decomposition is pinned against final HBM4E JEDEC geometry, which is an Open Question there and a TBD in its references. Those are the controller's internal geometry in any case, not the width of the port an engine drives. The one number with any source points the other way: bulk traffic on this port is a TDMA moving a tensor between HBM and TM, and the TM port is 1024 bits, so any other choice puts a width converter in the tensor path. That number is itself a choice, not architecture: noc_hs is registered at flavors: [unspecified], so there is no hs NoC specification standing behind it. DATA_WIDTH sets every bundle layout on the port and the byte-strobe width with it, so it cannot be left unstated -- but it should be read as a chosen default, not as architecture.
ssot_gap.assumed: DATA_WIDTH = 1024 bits (128 B), matching the TM port and the hs NoC beat rather than the DRAM burst granule; STRB_WIDTH = 128 follows it. This is a whole multiple of the 32 B BL8 burst the RFC mentions, so it does not contradict the DRAM-side numbers, but it is not derived from them. If HBM4E geometry later argues for 256 bits, the change is mechanical here (two parameters) and relayouts every bundle, so it should happen before RTL, not after.

ssot_gap.desc: The beat split leaves the geometry of a burst unstated, in two ways. (1) What are the units of `len`? A beat-based channel invites a beat count, and AXI would additionally bias it by one. Bytes, beats, and beats-minus-one are three different fields with the same name, and a mismatch between an initiator and a controller silently corrupts every transfer that is not a whole number of beats. (2) May a burst cross a 4 KB frame boundary? RFC-T100-0005 §3 makes the 4 KB frame the placement quantum and assigns `(side, stack, frame)` per frame, so two adjacent frames of one tensor need not be on one stack -- which means a contiguous stack-local run longer than a frame is only meaningful if the allocator happened to place the frames adjacently. Nothing states whether an initiator may rely on that, nor what a controller does mid-burst when the next beat would leave the frame: truncate, fault the remaining beats, or split. Related: the port cannot report either failure, because HbmStatus has no protocol-error code -- a `len` that disagrees with the beats actually sent is undetectable on the wire.
ssot_gap.assumed: `len` is a byte count, unbiased, and the beat count is ceil(len / (DATA_WIDTH/8)) -- derived by both ends, never sent. This matches the TM port so that a DMA driving both does not switch conventions mid-transfer. No frame-crossing rule is enforced: the port permits a burst of any `len` and an initiator that needs a same-stack guarantee splits the transfer itself, which is the same responsibility the stack-selection gap already leaves with it.

host_bar0.name: host_bar0
host_bar0.desc: Host-facing BAR0 ingress: BAR0-mapped SQ/CQ rings, posted doorbells, and max-merge fence banks. One submission is accepted on the SQ channel and completed out-of-line on the CQ channel.
host_bar0.notes: Doorbell writes are posted -- the host gets no completion, it polls the CQ or a fence. Fence reads are the only ordering guarantee the host has, so the HIB must not report a fence value before the underlying write is visible in TM or HBM. Completions are matched to submissions on `slot`, never on arrival order.

parameter.name: SQ_OPCODE_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Submission opcode. The four opcodes below need two bits, but the ch 11 SQ packet gives `opcode` a whole byte (byte 0 of the 32-byte packet), so eight is the field a device decodes; narrowing to 2 would describe a wire nothing drives.

parameter.name: SLOT_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Ring slot index, echoed on the completion. Bounded by the ring depth, and Q_CFG.SQ_DEPTH is a 16-bit field in t100_bar0.rdl, so a slot index that can address any legal depth is 16 bits.

parameter.name: REGION_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Region handle. 32 bits, the width of `region_id` in both the ch 11 KICK payload and the CQE.

parameter.name: ARG_WIDTH
parameter.desc: One opcode-specific operand. 64 bits because the operands are addresses -- ch 11's DMA payload carries `src_addr` / `dst_addr` as 64-bit fields -- and a 64-bit address space cannot be described by a narrower one.

parameter.name: LEN_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Transfer length in bytes. Ch 11's DMA payload field is `len_bytes`, 32 bits, and that is the width a device decodes, so this follows the byte image. It caps one entry at 4 GiB - 1 -- see G25.

parameter.name: SIGNAL_ID_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Fence bank index. 16 bits normatively: t100_bar0.rdl's FENCE_CAP states that the architectural fence id is 16 bits and sizes FENCE_BANK_DEPTH as a 16-bit field (<= 65536), so an implemented bank can grow with no wire change.

parameter.name: CQ_STATUS_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Completion status. 16 bits, the width of `status` in the ch 11 CQE image (bytes 4-5). The four codes below need two bits; the field a device writes is a halfword.

parameter.name: RESULT_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Opcode-specific completion return. Kept at 64 bits: `fence_read` returns a fence value, fence values on this interface are 64 bits, and a 32-bit result -- which is what the ch 11 CQE image has -- cannot carry what this contract's own opcode list asks it to return. See G25.

parameter.name: QUEUE_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Doorbell queue-context selector. The one width here with no normative source: nothing specifies a queue count, and page 0 of t100_bar0.rdl has a single SQ_TAIL / CQ_HEAD doorbell pair with no per-queue stride. 16 bits -- see G9.

parameter.name: RING_INDEX_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Producer / consumer index carried by a doorbell. 32 bits from the register that receives it: SQ_TAIL.VAL[31:0] in t100_bar0.rdl.

parameter.name: FENCE_VALUE_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Fence value. Monotonic and max-merged, so it must not wrap over a run; 64 bits matches ch 11's WAIT `target[]`.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Interface clock, HIB side. All signals sampled on the rising edge.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. CTRL.RESET drains and re-initialises the rings behind it (t100_bar0.rdl); this is the wire-level reset, not that register.

enum.name: SqOpcode
enum.desc: What a submission-queue entry asks the device to do.

member.name: dma
member.desc: Move data between host memory and device memory; `arg[0]` / `arg[1]` are source and destination, `len` the byte count.

member.name: launch_region
member.desc: Start work on `region`.

member.name: wait
member.desc: Gate on a fence reaching a value.

member.name: fence_read
member.desc: Read a fence bank back to the host; the value returns in the completion's `result`.

enum.name: CqStatus
enum.desc: How the operation a completion reports ended.

member.name: ok
member.desc: Completed normally. Agrees with ch 11's '0 = T100_OK'; the other three do not appear in ch 11 under these names, see G1.

member.name: bad_region
member.desc: `region` did not resolve, or resolved to something this opcode cannot act on.

member.name: bad_opcode
member.desc: `opcode` is not one this device implements.

member.name: fault
member.desc: Execution fault (access violation, ECC, downstream error). `result` carries the fault detail.

sq.desc: One host submission-queue entry: what to do, which region it belongs to, its operands, and the fence to advance when it completes.

signal.name: opcode
signal.desc: Host-visible work type. Which of `arg`, `len` and `region` mean anything is opcode-specific and is not tabulated anywhere; see G25.

signal.name: slot
signal.desc: Ring slot, echoed in the completion so the host can match a completion to its submission rather than to an arrival order.

signal.name: region
signal.desc: Region handle this work belongs to.

signal.name: arg
signal.desc: Two opcode-specific operands (e.g. DMA source and destination). One arrayed field rather than `arg0`/`arg1`: they are the same field indexed twice, and Packed's get_at/set_at is how a consumer should reach them.

signal.name: len
signal.desc: Byte count for opcodes that move data; ignored otherwise.

signal.name: signal_id
signal.desc: Fence bank to advance on completion. The entry names the fence but carries no value to advance it to -- see G3.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Submission valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Device accepts the submission. Acceptance is not completion: the outcome arrives later on the CQ channel.

cq.desc: One completion-queue entry: which slot completed, how it ended, and its opcode-specific return.

signal.name: slot
signal.desc: The `slot` of the submission being completed.

signal.name: status
signal.desc: Outcome.

signal.name: result
signal.desc: Opcode-specific return: the fence value for `fence_read`, and on `fault` the ch 11 fault detail (engine id in bits 7:0, failing opcode in 15:8, region-relative command index in 31:16). The numeric id spaces are unsettled; see G6.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Completion valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Host accepts the completion.

db.desc: Posted write announcing new submission-queue entries. One index write publishes a whole batch.

signal.name: queue
signal.desc: Queue context being rung. Only context 0 is implemented -- see G9.

signal.name: tail
signal.desc: New producer index. The ring depth is a power of two so the index wraps by mask (t100_bar0.rdl, Q_CFG).

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Doorbell write valid. Posted: there is no ready and no response.

fence.desc: Max-merge fence bank update, readable by the host.

signal.name: signal_id
signal.desc: Which fence bank to update.

signal.name: value
signal.desc: Monotonic value; the bank max-merges it, so a late duplicate is harmless and an out-of-order update cannot move a fence backwards.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Fence update valid.

ssot_gap.desc: Which SQ/CQ layout is normative? This contract and the ch 11 byte image transcribed in iface/t100/t100_wire.h are two different shapes for the same rings. The packet there is 32 bytes with an 8-byte common header carrying `cmd_id` and `flags`, and this contract has no field for either; and the two disagree on the width of DMA `len_bytes` and of the CQE `result`. Neither shape is machine-readable, so nothing decides which bytes a host and a device must agree on -- and they are co-developed against these exact fields.
ssot_gap.assumed: The field set is as written here -- no `cmd_id`, no `flags`. Where a width was open, the byte image wins: `len` is 32 bits. `result` is the exception and stays 64, because this contract's own `fence_read` opcode returns a fence value and fence values here are 64 bits, which a 32-bit result cannot carry.

ssot_gap.desc: The `opcode` and `status` codes are pinned nowhere machine-readable -- ch 11 lists names in prose tables and assigns no numbers -- and the two hand transcriptions already disagree about the SET, not just the values. iface/t100/t100_wire.h carries ch 11's opcodes as NOP, SET_REG, GET_REG, DMA, KICK, TELEMETRY, DFE_EXEC, WAIT, SIGNAL and its statuses as T100_OK plus nine T100_ERR_* names; neither matches the four of each declared here. A co-developed host and device must agree on these numbers, and prose cannot make them.
ssot_gap.assumed: Four opcodes and four statuses at values 0..3, generated into `SqOpcode` / `CqStatus` so a consumer switches on them instead of declaring its own copy. Only `ok = 0` is corroborated (ch 11's '0 = T100_OK'); the rest are this file's assignment. Generating them is what G1 asks for and does not make them the right numbers. HTI's functional model does not include this header: it decodes the 32-byte ch 11 packet with its own SqOpcode (nop=0 .. signal=7) because this bundle has no consumer yet.

ssot_gap.desc: The CQE fault result assigns eight bits to an engine id and eight bits to an opcode, but chapter 11 does not enumerate either numeric space. The DFE ISA names functional groups rather than engine ids, and the host and device therefore have no canonical values to share.
ssot_gap.assumed: The host-interface implementation's current values are used locally. They are not treated as architectural until chapter 11 or a shared machine-readable contract assigns them.

ssot_gap.desc: What value does a completed submission raise its fence to? `signal_id` names the bank to advance, but nothing on the entry carries a value, and the completion `{fence_id, value}` tuple is itself open in ch 4 §4.4.2 (mandatory / optional / boundary-only). There is no room for a tuple on a submission, so the field pair the fence channel carries -- id and value -- cannot be expressed there.
ssot_gap.assumed: The ch 11 fence-0 contiguous watermark: a completion advances `signal_id` by an implicit ordinal rather than to a value the host chose. In-region ordering is left to the executor, not to a tuple.

ssot_gap.desc: How many queue contexts are there? `queue` selects one, but no count is specified and page 0 of t100_bar0.rdl has exactly one SQ_TAIL / CQ_HEAD doorbell pair with no per-queue stride -- so the field's range is unconstrained by anything normative while the register surface it rings admits one. Multi-context / SR-IOV is out of scope for v1.0, which is a scope decision, not an encoding.
ssot_gap.assumed: QUEUE_WIDTH is 16 bits and only `queue = 0` is exercised. A doorbell for any other value has nowhere to land in the page-0 map.

ms_buf.name: ms_buf
ms_buf.desc: Write port into the MS memory buffers on the MSIC. Address and data are separate channels (AXI-style aw/w/b); a tile is a burst of fixed-width beats with `last` on the final one, and every access names which of the two buffers it targets.
ms_buf.notes: Modelled on the tm port deliberately: an engine driving both should not convert shapes mid-transfer, and the send engine drives exactly both -- it reads its source tile out of TM and writes it here. The difference is the address, which is a buffer selector and an offset rather than a bank and an offset, because the two MS buffers are named by the ISA and banks are not.

parameter.name: DATA_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Beat width. Matched to tm's DATA_WIDTH rather than derived: the send engine reads its source from TM and writes it here, so equal widths are what let it forward a beat instead of repacking one. What the link actually carries is G82.

parameter.name: STRB_WIDTH
parameter.desc: One strobe bit per byte of a beat, so DATA_WIDTH / 8. Restated as a literal rather than derived because the schema has no expression form for a parameter default; tm's parameter of this name is written the same way for the same reason. The final beat of a tile that is not a whole number of beats is masked with it.

parameter.name: OFFSET_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Byte offset within the selected buffer. 16 bits reaches 64 KiB, which is the tile-buffer size RFC-INFRA-0004 gives the MSIC's BAR2 window -- the only number anywhere near this buffer. No chapter states it; see G81.

parameter.name: LEN_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Bytes in one transfer. Sized to hold any tile the descriptor can describe, not to the buffer -- an over-large transfer is a refusal the target reports, not one the wire prevents.

parameter.name: TAG_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Transaction id, echoed on `b`. Matches tm's TAG_WIDTH so an engine driving both can use one counter.

parameter.name: INITIATOR_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Which unit issued the write. Same width and the same non-canonical id space as tm's field of this name (tm G11).

enum.name: MsBuf
enum.desc: Which MS memory buffer. The two codes are the ISA's dst_type values 0b00001 and 0b00010, renumbered to 0 and 1 because this port carries only the two buffers -- dst_type's 0b00000 (tensor memory) never reaches this wire, and encoding a value that cannot occur would make an all-zero payload look like a legal target.

member.name: A

ssot_gap.desc: This whole port is derived from two table rows. Chapters 3 and 4 define ms_buf_a and ms_buf_b as 'MS Memory Buffer A/B. This is SRAM memory on the MSIC' and say nothing else about them, and no chapter covers the MSIC's side at all -- chapter 16 is four bullets about inter-OPU UCIe and PCIe, chapter 10's 'APIC / MSIC / EIC System Roles' is a heading with no body, and chapter 14, which would cover metasurface rewrite scheduling, is a title. So a destination the ISA can name has no described target.
ssot_gap.assumed: The buffers behave like a write-only, byte-addressed memory reachable over an AXI-shaped port, which is the weakest structure that makes SEND expressible at all. Every specific number below is separately gapped; this entry is the statement that the port as a whole is inferred rather than transcribed.

ssot_gap.desc: How big is a buffer, and where in it does a tile land? SEND names a buffer and a source descriptor, and no field of the instruction names a destination offset -- dst_type is five bits selecting an interface, not an address. So either each SEND fills its buffer from zero, in which case two SENDs to buffer A cannot both be resident and the ping-pong is between A and B rather than within one, or there is a destination pointer somewhere the ISA does not show. The two readings differ observably: chapter 5's worked example sends two weight tiles to buffer A before one MSLOADA, which the fill-from-zero reading cannot express.
ssot_gap.assumed: Addressed, with the offset on this channel supplied by the engine, and a 64 KiB buffer -- the size RFC-INFRA-0004 gives the MSIC's BAR2 tile buffer, which is the only number anywhere near this memory and is an infrastructure draft rather than a chapter. Chosen because chapter 5's two-tiles-then-load example requires it: fill-from-zero would have the second SEND overwrite the first.

ssot_gap.desc: What is the link underneath, and how wide is it? The instruction type is UCIE and the EIC block diagram routes the MS DMA through an 'MSIC interface' to 40-80 SERDES lanes at 112 Gb/s -- and the diagram review flags that the datasheet calls the same link UCIe, so two artifacts disagree about the physical layer. RFC-INFRA-0004 describes a third shape, FABIO, in 32-bit beats of 1..16 with 8 credits each way, as an FMOD-level contract and explicitly not a bit-accurate one. No chapter states any of it.
ssot_gap.assumed: 1024-bit beats, matching tm, so the send engine forwards a beat rather than repacking one. This is a modelling choice about where the width conversion happens and not a claim about the link: whatever the physical layer turns out to be, it is below this port, and the credit and flit questions belong to that layer.

ssot_gap.desc: When is a written tile visible to MSLOADA, and what stops a SEND overwriting a buffer being read? Chapter 4 4.2.8 states the visibility rule for HBM -- a write's completion token means the bytes are globally visible -- and chapter 11 11.3.2 restates it for DMA completions and fences. Neither mentions the MS buffers. What chapter 4 does give this path is msync, 'resolved when the metasurface settling delay has expired', which orders an OVMM after a SEND's load; it says nothing about ordering a SEND after a load, which is the direction that matters for reuse.
ssot_gap.assumed: The `b` response means the bytes are in the buffer and a subsequent MSLOADA would see them, by analogy with 4.2.8 -- the same rule the tdma and host_dma models enforce on their write ports, applied to the only other write port an engine has. The `busy` status exists for the reverse direction but nothing generates it: with no described load-in-progress signal, an engine cannot know, so a SEND to a buffer under load is a hazard this port can report and not one it can prevent.

parameter.name: TAG_WIDTH

pcr.name: pcr
pcr.desc: Power / clock / reset domain control. One command per domain names the clock and reset state it should hold; the status channel reports the state PCR latched, which is not always the state that was asked for.
pcr.notes: A command that deasserts reset without enabling the clock is a sequencing bug, not a request PCR can serve: the status channel echoes the unchanged state and the model asserts. That asymmetry is the reason status is a channel rather than a return value -- a refused command still produces one, carrying what PCR kept.

enum.name: Domain
enum.desc: Which clock/reset domain a command addresses. Four, named after the register map (ssot/regs/pcr_regs.rdl DOMAIN0..DOMAIN3) rather than numbered here -- a fifth domain is a wire change and a compile error at every consumer, which is the intent.

member.name: management
member.desc: Always-on: the RoT, boot sequencing, PCR itself. Never gated, so a command naming it is a configuration error the architecture does not yet describe (G31).

member.name: compute
member.desc: The engine blocks: DFE, the tensor engines, VPU, XPU, OVMM.

member.name: memory
member.desc: Tensor memory and the HBM controllers.

member.name: io
member.desc: PCIe, UCIe, the SerDes and the host interface.

parameter.name: DOMAIN_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Domain selector width. Exactly the two bits the four named domains need -- not rounded up to a byte, because a value that is not a domain should not be expressible on the wire.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Interface clock. All signals sampled on the rising edge. This is the always-on domain's clock: PCR cannot be gated by a domain it controls.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. On deassertion every domain is clock-gated with reset held, which is the only safe power-on state -- a domain that came up released would be running before its clock was characterized.

ctl.desc: One domain command: which domain, and the clock and reset state it should hold.

signal.name: domain
signal.desc: Which domain this command addresses.

signal.name: clock_enable
signal.desc: 1 = run the domain's clock, 0 = gate it.

signal.name: reset_assert
signal.desc: 1 = hold the domain in reset, 0 = release it. Defaults asserted: an unfilled command holds a domain down rather than releasing it.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Command valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: PCR accepts the command. Acceptance is not agreement -- an illegal command is accepted and then refused on the status channel.

status.desc: The clock and reset state PCR holds for the commanded domain, after applying the command or refusing it.

signal.name: domain
signal.desc: The domain this status describes. Same type as the command's, so the two compare without a cast.

signal.name: clock_enable
signal.desc: 1 = the domain's clock is running. Reads back the DOMAIN<n>.CLOCK_EN latch.

signal.name: reset_assert
signal.desc: 1 = the domain is held in reset. Reads back the DOMAIN<n>.RESET_ASSERT latch.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Status valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: The boot sequencer accepts the status.

ssot_gap.desc: Are four domains the chip's domain map? The count comes from ssot/regs/pcr_regs.rdl, which declares DOMAIN0..DOMAIN3 and names them management / compute / memory / IO. That reads like intent rather than a placeholder, but no architectural document states a domain map, so it could equally be four registers written to have something to model. Related: nothing says whether the always-on domain may be commanded at all -- it is by definition ungateable, so a command naming it is either rejected, ignored, or a fault, and the three are indistinguishable here.
ssot_gap.assumed: The four named domains are the map, and DOMAIN_WIDTH is sized to exactly them. A command naming `management` is accepted and applied like any other, because refusing it would need an error code the status channel does not have (G33).

ssot_gap.desc: How is 'powered but not clocked' expressed? The channel carries clock and reset only. A power domain is not the same thing as a clock domain -- a block can be powered and gated, or fully power-gated with its state lost -- and the difference is exactly what a boot sequencer has to walk. With no power bit, `clock_enable` has to stand in for 'the domain is up', which makes a power-gated domain and a clock-gated one the same value on the wire.
ssot_gap.assumed: clock_enable is the only 'domain is up' the port can express. The illegal-release check reads it as such: reset released while the clock is gated is a sequencing bug. Power state is not modelled.

ssot_gap.desc: How does PCR refuse a command? The status channel carries the same three fields as the command, so a refusal is reported as an unchanged state and nothing more -- the initiator has to remember what it asked for and diff. That also makes two different refusals identical on the wire: a release-without-clock sequencing error and a domain that failed to come up both read as 'still held'. A status code would separate them; there is none.
ssot_gap.assumed: Refusal is 'echo the unchanged state, then assert'. The model asserts rather than coping, on the grounds that a boot sequencer issuing an illegal transition is a bug to catch in simulation rather than a runtime condition to report.

ssot_gap.desc: Where does per-BLOCK release live? `mgmt.yaml` also declares `BootRelease` (block_id, phase, release), which is per block and per boot phase, while this port is per domain. Both exist and neither references the other, so it is unstated whether a block leaves reset when its domain is released, when its BootRelease arrives, or when both -- and the ordering between the two paths is exactly what a boot sequence is.
ssot_gap.assumed: The two are independent and BootRelease is not on this port. A block observes its domain's reset only; per-block release is unmodelled until the boot sequence controller has a unit.

region_admit.name: region_admit
region_admit.desc: The KICK handoff: HTI admits one region to the front-end processor by naming its command buffer, and the front end reports back how the region ended. Three fields down, two up.
region_admit.notes: This is deliberately not the submission-queue entry. Chapter 2 2.3.2 hands the front end `{region_id, cmd_buf_addr, cmd_buf_bytes}` and an interrupt -- not an SQ packet -- and chapter 11 11.1.2 step 6 has HTI, not the front end, write the terminal CQE. So the front end never sees an opcode, a ring slot, or a fence id, and cannot complete a submission; it runs a command buffer and says how that went. Modelling this seam by forwarding host_bar0 records across it is what made the front end look like it owned a doorbell and a fence bank (see models#248).

parameter.name: REGION_ID_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Region handle width. 32, matching `region_id` in both the chapter 11 KICK payload and the CQE -- and matching host_bar0's own `region`, because it is the same handle travelling further in.

parameter.name: ADDR_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Command-buffer address width. An HBM address, and a 64-bit address space cannot be described by a narrower field.

parameter.name: LEN_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Command-buffer length in bytes. 32 to match host_bar0's `len`, which is where the number comes from when the host DMAs the buffer in.

parameter.name: STATUS_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Region outcome width. 16, the width of `status` in the chapter 11 CQE image (bytes 4-5), because this value is copied into that field unchanged.

enum.name: RegionStatus
enum.desc: How a region ended. A region latches its FIRST fault and quiesces (chapter 2 2.3.2), so this is the first thing that went wrong and not a summary of everything that did. The codes are deliberately the same shape as host_bar0's CqStatus -- HTI copies this value into the terminal CQE -- but they are declared separately here; see G45.

member.name: ok
member.desc: The command stream drained and every output write is visible. The only outcome that means the region's results may be read.

member.name: bad_buffer
member.desc: `cmd_buf_addr` / `cmd_buf_bytes` did not describe a command buffer this front end could walk -- unreachable, unaligned, or a length that is not a whole number of commands.

member.name: bad_command
member.desc: A command in the buffer is not one this front end implements. The region stops here rather than skipping it, because a command buffer is a program and skipping one silently changes what it computes.

member.name: fault
member.desc: Execution fault reported from downstream, or raised while walking. Distinguished from bad_command in that the buffer was legal and something failed anyway.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Interface clock. Both channels sampled on the rising edge.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low. A region in flight across reset is abandoned, not resumed: its command buffer is still resident but the walk's position is not architectural state.

kick.desc: One admitted region: its handle, and where its command buffer lives.

signal.name: region_id
signal.desc: Host-assigned region handle, echoed on the report and from there into the terminal CQE. Unique among a context's live regions and reused only after that CQE is reaped, so it identifies the region for as long as anything can refer to it.

signal.name: cmd_buf_addr
signal.desc: HBM address of the resident LLIR command buffer. Resident is the point: the host DMA'd it once and a region may be re-kicked against it many times with new activations, so this is a pointer to state that outlives the region.

signal.name: cmd_buf_bytes
signal.desc: Command-buffer length in bytes. The only bound on the walk -- there is no terminator command -- which is why a wrong length is a bad_buffer rather than a run that stops somewhere plausible.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Admission valid. This is the interrupt of chapter 2 2.3.2: the handshake is the wake, so there is no separate interrupt signal on this port.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: The front end accepts the region. Withheld while it is walking one, which is what serialises regions -- chapter 11 says the front end issues regions in program order, so a second admission waits rather than interleaving.

report.desc: How the region ended. HTI turns this into the terminal KICK CQE; the front end does not write completions itself.

signal.name: region_id
signal.desc: The region this report is about. Echoed rather than implied, so the two are checkable against each other even though only one region is admitted at a time.

signal.name: status
signal.desc: The region's first fault, or ok. Copied into the terminal CQE's `status` unchanged, which is why it is the CQE's width and not narrowed to the four codes.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Report valid. Raised when the command stream has drained AND the region's output writes are visible -- not when the last command was issued. The gap between the two is real, and reporting at the wrong end of it would let a host read outputs that have not landed.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: HTI accepts the report. It reserved a CQ slot before admitting the region (chapter 11 11.1.2 step 5), so it can always take one -- which is what guarantees a terminal completion even for a region that faulted.

ssot_gap.desc: Should RegionStatus and host_bar0's CqStatus be one enum? HTI copies this status into the terminal CQE's `status` field, so the two are the same value space by construction, and declaring them twice means two lists that can drift into disagreeing about what code 2 means. They are separate here because an interface-owned enum cannot currently be referenced from another interface -- only ISA enums can, via `enum = { spec, type }`. host_bar0's own G1 already records that three of its four CqStatus codes do not appear in chapter 11 under those names, so the shared list is not yet pinned to the spec either.
ssot_gap.assumed: The codes agree by inspection, and the four here are the four there. The real fix is one enum in one place, which is what models#243 sets up by deriving these specs from the chapter that defines T100_ERR_*.

ssot_gap.desc: Can more than one region be admitted at a time? Chapter 2 2.3.2 says consecutive regions may overlap at their boundary in v1.0 -- 'a region boundary is a scheduling seam, not a barrier' -- and chapter 11 says the front end issues regions in program order with boundary overlap. Overlap at a boundary implies the front end holds two regions at once, at least briefly, but this port has no way to say which region an instruction belongs to and no second `region_id` in flight. Withholding `ready` while walking makes the overlap impossible; accepting a second admission makes the report ambiguous without a tag.
ssot_gap.assumed: One at a time: `ready` is withheld while walking, so the boundary overlap v1.0 permits is not modelled. That is the conservative direction -- it serialises work that hardware may pipeline, costing throughput in the model rather than correctness.
