tdma.name: tdma
tdma.desc: DFE -> TDMA dispatch port: carries a decoded TDMA instruction (MREAD, MWRITE, MZERO, DLOAD or DSTORE, plus the strided aliases) with its resolved source and destination descriptors, the 42-bit HBM address the descriptor-move instructions name, and the identity the engine quotes back on completion.
tdma.notes: Opcodes and field widths follow ssot/isa/dfe_isa.toml. Completion/retire signaling (needed for ctl_type dsync) travels on the separate `completion` interface, and the cqid and descriptor ids here are what let the engine populate it -- 4.2.8.1 has the cqid 'ride through the DFSC and the execution unit', and Table 4.2.8 builds the token out of the ids, so an engine handed only resolved descriptors could answer neither. `addr` was previously absent and its mapping called 'unit-model policy'; it is an instruction field (dfe_isa.toml field_type.addr, 42 bits) that DLOAD and DSTORE cannot be executed without, so it belongs on the wire rather than in a convention.

parameter.name: DESC_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Descriptor payload width: one tensor descriptor. Sized from the descriptor spec rather than typed here -- it moved from 32 to 64 bytes upstream and the hand-typed 256 did not follow.

parameter.name: TID_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Descriptor-index width, matching the ISA's src0/dst fields and the completion port's ids.

parameter.name: CQID_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Completion-queue id width. 4.2.8.1: 'an 8-bit completion id (cqid[7:0], plus a wrap bit for full/empty detection)'. The wrap bit stays inside the DFE.

parameter.name: ADDR_WIDTH
parameter.desc: HBM address width for the descriptor-move instructions, from dfe_isa.toml field_type.addr. Chapter 4 line 37: 'A 42-bit HBM address is specified in the descriptor load, DLOAD, and store, DSTORE, instructions giving the compiler the flexibility to organize descriptors as it sees fit.' Matches hbm_interface's ADDR_WIDTH, which is the port this address is issued on.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Interface clock. All signals sampled on the rising edge.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset.

cmd.desc: Dispatched TDMA instruction: opcode, the DFCQ id and descriptor ids to quote back, resolved src/dst descriptors, and the HBM address DLOAD/DSTORE name.

signal.name: op
signal.desc: Instruction opcode. MREAD/MWRITE/MZERO/DLOAD/DSTORE are dispatched on this port; the strided variants are bit-identical aliases, so this field does not distinguish them -- 'strided vs contiguous is selected by the descriptor' (dfe_isa.toml).

signal.name: cqid
signal.desc: DFCQ entry id allocated at decode. Rides through the engine untouched and comes back on the completion port, where it sets that entry's `complete` bit (4.2.8.1). The engine does not interpret it.

signal.name: src_id
signal.desc: Descriptor index `src` was resolved from, for the engine to return in the completion token's src0 field; valid when src_id_v is set.

signal.name: src_id_v
signal.desc: The instruction has a source. Clear for MZERO and DLOAD, which have no src0 field at all. An explicit bit rather than an all-zero descriptor: descriptor 0 is a legal DFRT entry, so 'reads descriptor 0' and 'reads nothing' must be distinguishable, which is the same reason Table 4.2.8 carries valid bits.

signal.name: src
signal.desc: Source descriptor, resolved from the instruction's src0 descriptor index. Meaningful only when src_id_v is set. Which memory it names is the opcode's business, not this field's: MREAD sources HBM, MWRITE and DSTORE source tensor memory and the DFDT respectively.

signal.name: dst_id
signal.desc: Descriptor index `dst` was resolved from, for the engine to return in the completion token's dst field; valid when dst_id_v is set.

signal.name: dst_id_v
signal.desc: The instruction has a destination. Clear for DSTORE, whose destination is an HBM address rather than a descriptor.

signal.name: dst
signal.desc: Destination descriptor, resolved from the instruction's dst descriptor index. Meaningful only when dst_id_v is set.

signal.name: addr
signal.desc: The HBM address DLOAD reads a descriptor from and DSTORE writes one to, taken verbatim from the instruction's `addr` field. Zero and meaningless for every other opcode on this port.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Command valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Command ready (asserted by the TDMA engine).

ssot_gap.desc: DLOAD has nowhere to put what it loads. The instruction's whole purpose is to move a descriptor INTO the DFE: 'Load descriptor at addr from HBM into the Data Flow Descriptor Table (DFDT)' (dfe_isa.toml; chapter 4 line 282 says the same). But this port has no return path other than the completion token, which is three descriptor ids and a cqid, and the DFDT's ports are enumerated in 4.2.5.1 as '4 read ports - 2 x 64-byte source descriptors - 1 x 64-byte destination descriptor - 1 PC descriptor for the VCALL instruction or - 1 write port - 1 x 64-byte destination descriptor FOR TADVANCE'. One write port, spoken for. So the structure has no port for the write and the wire has no field for the data, while two places in the chapter say the instruction performs it. It is also the only TDMA instruction whose destination is not memory.
ssot_gap.assumed: DLOAD is refused by the engine and counted, rather than executed with a guessed-at delivery mechanism. The two candidate resolutions are visibly different hardware -- either the DFDT's write port is shared and this wire grows a 64-byte return payload, or DLOAD is not a TDMA instruction at all and the DFE fetches the descriptor itself -- and choosing one in a model would bake in a boundary the architecture has not drawn. DSTORE is unaffected: its source is a descriptor the DFE already resolved onto this wire, so writing it to HBM needs nothing new.

ssot_gap.desc: Nothing on this port distinguishes a strided transfer from a contiguous one, by design -- 'strided vs contiguous is selected by the descriptor' -- but the descriptor field that would select it is undefined. MSTREAD and MSTWRITE are declared bit-identical aliases of MREAD and MWRITE, so the opcode cannot say. That leaves the descriptor's `layout` field, which tensor_descriptor.toml documents as the 'DSFC layout selector (section 6)' -- and chapter 6's DSFC section is a stub. The descriptor also carries both `dims` (per-tensor extents) and `tdims` (per-tile extents) with no statement of the stride between tiles, which is precisely the number a strided transfer needs.
ssot_gap.assumed: Every transfer on this port is contiguous: `len` bytes from the source's base to the destination's base, with dims and layout unread. A strided transfer is not approximated -- a wrong stride writes the right number of bytes to the wrong places, which no test downstream would attribute to this engine.

tm.name: tm
tm.desc: Banked Tensor Memory read/write port. Address and data are separate channels (AXI-style ar/r/aw/w/b); a multi-byte transfer is a burst of fixed-width beats with `last` on the final one, and every access names its bank so the TM model can arbitrate.
tm.notes: Split transaction: a request carries a tag, the completion returns it. Ordering is per-tag, not global. `w` has no tag (as in AXI4), so write beats follow `aw` in issue order and two outstanding writes may not interleave their data. `bank` is echoed on `r` and `b` for convenience only; `tag` is the only sound pairing.

parameter.name: BANK_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Bank selector. 1024 banks is 10 bits. A bank is a PNM channel (see the banking ssot_gap), not an SRAM module.

parameter.name: OFFSET_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Byte offset within one bank. A bank is 1 MiB (bank_bytes = 1048576), so the address inside it is exactly 20 bits, which is also the per-PNM-channel address width PR #22 gives.

parameter.name: LEN_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Transfer length in BYTES, not beats -- see the burst-geometry ssot_gap. 21 bits, not 20: the largest legal span is a whole bank (2^20 bytes) and a plain count of 2^20 needs one more bit. AXI encodes length as beats-minus-one to avoid that; a bias is not used here because a byte count is the value the initiator, the byte-lane logic and the ELOG all already hold, and an off-by-one encoding on a port nine units drive is a defect waiting to happen.

parameter.name: DATA_WIDTH
parameter.desc: One beat. THIS NUMBER IS A CHOICE, NOT ARCHITECTURE. It is chosen to match the high-speed NoC, because bulk TM traffic arrives over that fabric and a TM port narrower or wider than the NoC beat would put a width converter on every tensor access. But noc_hs is registered at flavors: [unspecified] -- there is no hs NoC specification to match against yet. When noc_hs is specified, this becomes a from_spec reference and the number is either confirmed or corrected.

parameter.name: STRB_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Byte enables for one write beat, one bit per byte (DATA_WIDTH / 8). Its own parameter because the generator cannot yet evaluate an expression over another parameter; it must track DATA_WIDTH.

parameter.name: TAG_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Request tag, echoed on the completion. 32 bits -- wide enough that an initiator never has to reuse a tag while a request is outstanding, which is what per-tag ordering requires.

parameter.name: INITIATOR_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Initiator unit id, for ELOG attribution. Four bits allow every current TM initiator to have a distinct value. The id space is not yet canonical, so this interface fixes the width but does not invent an encoding.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Interface clock. All signals sampled on the rising edge.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset.

enum.name: TmStatus
enum.desc: How a tensor-memory access ended. Shared by the read-data and write-response channels.

member.name: ok
member.desc: Access completed normally.

member.name: bank_out_of_range
member.desc: `bank` is not in 0..1023.

member.name: span_crosses_bank
member.desc: The requested span left the bank it started in.

member.name: unaligned
member.desc: `offset` (or the span) violates an alignment the target requires.

ar.desc: Read request: which bank, where in it, how many bytes, and who is asking.

signal.name: bank
signal.desc: Bank to read (0..1023). The initiator declares it; the target arbitrates.

signal.name: offset
signal.desc: Byte offset of the first byte, within the bank.

signal.name: len
signal.desc: Bytes to read. 0 is not a legal request. A span must not cross a bank boundary; whether that survives the beat split is unsettled -- see the burst-geometry ssot_gap.

signal.name: tag
signal.desc: Echoed on every beat of the matching `r` burst. The only sound pairing between a request and its data, since ordering is per-tag.

signal.name: initiator
signal.desc: Unit id of the requester, for ELOG attribution and (later) per-initiator conflict accounting.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Read request valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: TM accepts the read request.

r.desc: One beat of read data, tagged, with a per-beat status and an end-of-burst marker.

signal.name: data
signal.desc: One beat of read data. On the final beat of a burst whose `len` is not a whole multiple of the beat, the bytes beyond `len` are undefined -- there is no read strobe to mask them.

signal.name: tag
signal.desc: The `tag` of the `ar` this beat belongs to. Every beat of a burst carries it.

signal.name: bank
signal.desc: The bank the data came from. Redundant with `tag`; do not pair on it.

signal.name: status
signal.desc: Outcome for THIS beat (like AXI's RRESP). Four bits for four codes, leaving room to add one without moving the bundle.

signal.name: last
signal.desc: Final beat of this burst. The consumer counts beats against it; nothing else on the channel says how long the burst is.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Read data valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Initiator accepts the beat.

aw.desc: Write request: which bank, where in it, how many bytes, and who is writing.

signal.name: bank
signal.desc: Bank to write (0..1023).

signal.name: offset
signal.desc: Byte offset of the first byte, within the bank.

signal.name: len
signal.desc: Bytes to write. 0 is not a legal request. Must agree with the number of `w` beats and their strobes; a disagreement is a protocol error the port cannot report, since `b.status` has no code for it.

signal.name: tag
signal.desc: Echoed on `b`. Required: a DMA cannot signal until TM has the data, and the acknowledgement is what tells it so.

signal.name: initiator
signal.desc: Unit id of the writer, for ELOG attribution.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Write request valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: TM accepts the write request.

w.desc: One beat of write data with byte strobes and an end-of-burst marker. Untagged: beats follow `aw` in issue order.

signal.name: data
signal.desc: One beat of write data. Bytes whose strobe is 0 are not written and their value is ignored.

signal.name: strobe
signal.desc: Byte enables for `data`, one bit per byte. This is how a transfer that is not a whole number of beats terminates: the final beat masks the bytes past `len`. All ones is a full-width beat.

signal.name: last
signal.desc: Final beat of this write burst. The target may not raise `b` before it.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Write data valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: TM accepts the beat.

b.desc: Write completion: one acknowledgement per accepted `aw`, raised no earlier than the beat carrying `w.last`.

signal.name: tag
signal.desc: The `tag` of the `aw` being completed.

signal.name: bank
signal.desc: The bank written. Redundant with `tag`.

signal.name: status
signal.desc: Outcome for the whole write. Same encoding as `r.status` -- one TmStatus means the same thing on both sides of the port by construction.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Write response valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Initiator accepts the response.

ssot_gap.desc: TM's address map is unspecified, so how a flat address picks a bank is undefined -- and the model's decode is probably wrong. The SIZE is right: T100_arch_spec PR #22 gives each Tensor Engine 16 MiB as 16 PNM Channels x 1 MiB with a 20-bit per-channel address, and 64 active TEs x 16 channels is exactly 1024 x 1 MiB = 1 GiB, so a `bank` here is a PNM channel and `offset` is its 20-bit address. The normative text is empty: pg ch 13 §13.2.1 (Tensor Memory) and §13.2.4 (SRAM Memory Map) are both one-line stubs. Three consequences. (a) Nothing says how a flat address picks a channel. §13.1.1 does specify the HBM side -- interleaved 8 bytes at a time across TEs, with equations -- so the TM analogue is precisely what is missing, and tdma's linear `bank = addr / bank_bytes` is almost certainly not it: it parks a contiguous MiB in one channel, serializing exactly the contiguous runs a DMA issues. (b) The conflict lives one level BELOW a channel: Memory inside a PNM channel is an 8x8 array of single-port modules, and a bank conflict is two of nine requesters (six reads, three writes) hitting one module in a clock -- which is why the hardware counter `tm_bank_conflict_inc[3:0]` counts 0..8. One `bank` field per request cannot express that, so bank-conflict cost is not modelable on this port as shaped. (c) xpu reads EngineCmd.descriptor as a bank id, so `bank` already means two things across initiators. The candidate resolution needs no interleave statement on this port at all: carry the flat offset and let the TM model decode, which makes both levels TM micro-architecture and deletes every initiator's decode.
ssot_gap.assumed: The linear decode is treated as a stub: `bank = addr / bank_bytes`, `offset = addr % bank_bytes`, with (bank, offset) on the wire as PR #22's channel and 20-bit channel address. Bank-conflict cost is not charged at all rather than charged wrongly. Resolution is the memory-model owner's, not an initiator's.

ssot_gap.desc: The beat split leaves the geometry of a burst unstated, in two ways. (1) What are the units of `len`? `len` is a byte count, but a beat-based channel invites a beat count, and AXI would additionally bias it by one. Bytes, beats, and beats-minus-one are three different fields with the same name, and a mismatch between an initiator and the target silently corrupts every transfer that is not a whole number of beats. (2) May a burst cross a bank boundary? A span must not, and TmStatus carries `span_crosses_bank` to report it -- but with a burst now spanning several beats and a bank being 1 MiB, the rule has to say WHICH boundary and what a target does mid-burst when the next beat would cross: truncate, fault the remaining beats, or split. Nothing says. Related: this port has no way to report a `len` that disagrees with the beats actually sent, because TmStatus has no code for a protocol error.
ssot_gap.assumed: `len` is a byte count, unbiased (so LEN_WIDTH is 21 bits to hold a full-bank span of 2^20), and the beat count is ceil(len / (DATA_WIDTH/8)) -- derived, never sent. A burst must stay inside one bank; an initiator that needs a run crossing a bank splits it into one transfer per bank, and a target that sees a crossing span rejects the whole transfer with `span_crosses_bank` rather than truncating it. Neither rule is new architecture.

ucie.name: ucie
ucie.desc: DFE -> UCIe send-engine dispatch port: carries a decoded SEND or TSEND instruction with its resolved source descriptor and destination interface selector.
ucie.notes: Opcodes and field widths follow ssot/isa/dfe_isa.toml. `dst` mirrors the instruction's 5-bit dst_type field (destination interface / memory type), not a descriptor.

parameter.name: DESC_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Descriptor payload width: one tensor descriptor. Sized from the descriptor spec rather than typed here -- it moved from 32 to 64 bytes upstream and the hand-typed 256 did not follow.

parameter.name: TID_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Descriptor-index width, matching the ISA's src0 field and the completion port's ids.

parameter.name: CQID_WIDTH
parameter.desc: Completion-queue id width. 4.2.8.1: 'an 8-bit completion id (cqid[7:0], plus a wrap bit for full/empty detection)'. The wrap bit stays inside the DFE.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Interface clock. All signals sampled on the rising edge.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset.

cmd.desc: Dispatched UCIe send instruction: opcode, resolved source descriptor, destination interface selector.

signal.name: op
signal.desc: Instruction opcode. Only SEND and TSEND are dispatched on this port.

signal.name: src
signal.desc: Source descriptor, resolved from the instruction's src0 descriptor index (SRAM source of the send).

signal.name: dst
signal.desc: Destination interface / memory type, verbatim from the instruction's dst_type field.

signal.name: cqid
signal.desc: DFCQ entry id allocated at decode. Rides through the engine untouched and comes back on the completion port, where it sets that entry's `complete` bit (4.2.8.1). The engine does not interpret it.

signal.name: src_id
signal.desc: Descriptor index `src` was resolved from, for the engine to return in the completion token's src0 field; valid when src_id_v is set.

signal.name: src_id_v
signal.desc: The instruction has a source. Always set for SEND and TSEND -- both have a src0 -- but carried explicitly rather than assumed, because descriptor 0 is a legal DFRT entry and 'reads descriptor 0' must stay distinguishable from 'reads nothing', which is the same reason Table 4.2.8 carries valid bits.

signal.name: valid
signal.desc: Command valid.

signal.name: ready
signal.desc: Command ready (asserted by the UCIe send engine).

ssot_gap.desc: Does a SEND set a DFRT ready bit, and if so on a descriptor naming what? 4.2.3 names SEND among the units whose completion info 'contains the destination descriptor' and is used to set a DFRT ready bit. The encoding says otherwise, and it says so in this file's own declared source: dfe_isa.toml gives SEND and TSEND the fields { opcode, src0, dst_type@30 } and no dst, which is what chapter 3's §3.3 table renders (63..35 reserved | 34..30 dst_type | 29..14 reserved | 13..6 src0 | 5..0 opcode) and what 4.2.4's overlay repeats. A destination descriptor also could not name an MS buffer if there were a field for one: chapter 2's AST nibble is 0x0 HBM / 0x1 TM, with 0x2..0xF reserved. So 4.2.3's list contradicts the instruction the compiler actually writes.
ssot_gap.assumed: dstv is clear, on the authority of dfe_isa.toml rather than of a model choice -- this port carries no dst_id because the instruction has no dst to fill it from. Consequence recorded rather than hidden: a SEND is not a producer in the DFRT sense, so the OVMM chapter 5 shows waiting for its weight tiles is ordered only by msync -- a timer rather than a dependency on the send that filled the buffer. Asked upstream as T100_arch_spec#70, now as a documentation contradiction in 4.2.3 rather than an unanswered layout. Not blocking: flipping dstv would mean changing the ISA spec, not this port's assumption.

ssot_gap.desc: No transfer length, and two readings of the descriptor that differ. The port carries one resolved 64-byte tensor descriptor and no byte count, so how many bytes a SEND moves has to be computed from the descriptor's fields -- and the descriptor carries both `dims` (the tensor) and `tdims` (the tile) with nothing stating which one a send moves. This is the same silence the tdma reads as tdims (its G69) and the xpu reads as tdims (its G63); it recurs here because it is a property of the descriptor rather than of any one engine.
ssot_gap.assumed: One tile: tdims[0] * tdims[1] * element width, the same reading the other two engines take. Consistency across the three is the argument, not evidence -- the whole-tensor reading would need a tile-array stride that chapter 6's DSFC section does not define.

ssot_gap.desc: What does TSEND transpose, and how does that differ from the XPU? 4.2.5.2 gives TSEND one clause -- 'TSEND transposes the data before sending' -- with no statement of what the transposed shape is, whether it applies to the tile or the tensor, or which dimensions swap for a rank above two. Meanwhile the XPU is described as the transpose unit and takes its own dispatch port. So the die has two transposers, one of which is a side effect of a send, and nothing distinguishes when a compiler should use which.
ssot_gap.assumed: TSEND swaps the tile's two extents, so the same bytes leave in column-major order, and the length is unchanged. The overlap with the XPU is left as it is: nothing here needs resolving to model a send, and inventing a distinction would be inventing the answer.

dfe.name: dfe
dfe.desc: Data Flow Engine: fetches and decodes the DFE instruction stream (isa/dfe_isa.toml), resolves descriptor indices against the DFDT, and dispatches to the TDMA engine, the UCIe send engine, and the execution units (OVMM/VPU/XPU); tracks retirement via the completion port.
dfe.notes: Instructions arrive from the FEP, on-die, over AXI-Lite -- not from the host at the chip edge. Chapter 4 4.2.2 is explicit about all three: the requester is the FEP, the bus is AXI-Lite, and a full FIFO is handled by deasserting READY. That makes the ingress port's backpressure the only flow control, which is why no credit or overrun appears anywhere on this boundary (see G42). The address map below is a DUMMY placeholder: decode windows and bases are invented for tooling bring-up and do not reflect the real memory map, and the spec routes by opcode rather than by address (G44). Dispatch/completion ports are internal; their peer wiring is declared by the parent via [connection]. The csr port is model-only telemetry: the architecture gives the DFE a BAR0 page-1 register window but no offsets yet (G95), so nothing behind that port is an ABI.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: DFE core clock; all boundary interfaces are synchronous to it.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. Chapter 4 describes no reset behaviour; what the model abandons and why that is safe is recorded as G96.

interface.name: cfg_axi
interface.desc: Named by 04-dataflow-engine.md 4.2.2. The instruction ingress: 64-bit writes from the FEP into the instruction FIFO, plus the DFDT and CSR windows in the same address space. This unit is the AXI responder -- 'the FEP has an AXI Lite requester interface, through which it sends 64-bit data to DFE, which has an AXI responder interface'. Backpressure is the whole flow control -- when the FIFO has no free entry the responder withholds AWREADY/WREADY and the requester's store stalls, so there is no credit to read and no overrun to report.

interface.name: tdma
interface.desc: Named by 04-dataflow-engine.md 4.2.6 (the TDMA instruction FIFO; instruction types in 4.2.5.2). Dispatch port to the TDMA engine (MREAD/MWRITE/MSTREAD/MSTWRITE/MZERO/DLOAD/DSTORE); this unit initiates because the transmit stage steers issued instructions onto it.

interface.name: eu_ovmm
interface.desc: Named by 04-dataflow-engine.md 4.2.6 (the OVMM instruction FIFO; instruction types in 4.2.5.2). Dispatch port to the OVMM execution unit (op=OVMM).

interface.name: eu_vpu
interface.desc: Named by 04-dataflow-engine.md 4.2.6 (the VPU instruction FIFO; instruction types in 4.2.5.2). Dispatch port to the VPU (op=VCALL; vpu_kernel_addr valid).

interface.name: eu_xpu
interface.desc: Named by 04-dataflow-engine.md 4.2.6 (the XPU instruction FIFO; instruction types in 4.2.5.2). Dispatch port to the XPU (op=XPU).

interface.name: ucie
interface.desc: Named by 04-dataflow-engine.md 4.2.6 (the SEND instruction FIFO; instruction types in 4.2.5.2). Dispatch port to the UCIe send engine (SEND/TSEND).

interface.name: cmp
interface.desc: Named by 04-dataflow-engine.md 4.2.8: 'completion tokens are returned from TDMA, OVMM, VPU, XPU and SEND units'. Retirement report port (units drive payload/valid; DFE drives ready). Fan-in arbitration across completing units is parent wiring policy.

interface.name: csr
interface.desc: A telemetry window, and nothing architectural yet. Every register behind it is model-only (G95): chapter 11 Table 11-2 gives the DFE BAR0 page 1 and chapters 4 and 17 name three registers on it (DESC_TABLE_BASE, last_write_count, last_read_count), but no revision of the SystemRDL places them -- so this RDL carries only what makes the block diagnosable from outside (operations completed, refusals, last outcome) and deliberately none of the named registers at an invented offset.

ssot_gap.desc: Is READY-deassert the settled flow control, or a placeholder? Chapter 4 4.2.2 states it plainly -- 'when there are no entries available in the FIFO, the READY signal to the AXI Lite requester interface is deasserted to prevent FEP from writing a new instruction' -- so the landed architecture has no credit and no overrun. But a FEP-readable credit counter is an open review proposal (H7 in review_greg_2026_07_08/24-hti-in-firmware.md, on greg/host-interface-review-2026-07-08, unmerged), on the grounds that firmware should never issue a store that can stall. The two are not equivalent for a model: READY is backpressure a bounded fifo gives for free, while a credit counter is a register the requester polls and can get wrong.
ssot_gap.assumed: READY-deassert, per the landed chapter. The instruction port is an ordinary bounded fifo and the requester simply blocks. If H7 lands it should arrive as a diagnostic counter beside the backpressure rather than as a replacement for it -- a credit that firmware may ignore does not remove the need for the FIFO to be able to say no.

ssot_gap.desc: Does the HIB also write instructions here, and if so how are two requesters arbitrated? Chapter 4 4.2.1 says 'the front end processor (FEP) and the host interface block (HIB) may have a route to reach the DFE', and images/DFE_Block_Diagram.md is firmer -- 'an operator is written into the DFE from either the FEP or the host interface (HIB) over a 64-bit AXI bus'. Neither says whether that is two requesters onto one responder, needing arbitration inside this unit, or a second port. 'May have a route' is not a commitment, and the difference is a port on this boundary.
ssot_gap.assumed: One requester, the FEP. The port is declared once and the assembly wires the FEP to it. If the HIB route is real it is the same shape as the CSR fabric's two initiators, which this repo already arbitrates fixed-priority -- but choosing that now would invent a priority the architecture has not stated.

ssot_gap.desc: What selects the dispatch target -- the write address or the opcode? The address map below decodes the write address into a per-engine window, which is how the model routes today and is marked dummy. The architecture does not work that way: chapter 4 has the FEP store every instruction to one place ('a cacheable address in DFE's SRAM address space'), and the ISA's opcode is what names the engine. So the address windows are scaffolding standing in for a decode that belongs to the instruction. Chapter 12 disagrees with chapter 4 on the address besides -- a fixed FE_CMD_ADDR reached by non-temporal store, into an 'operator queue, OPQ', where chapter 4 says a cacheable address into the 'instruction FIFO'. Cacheable and non-temporal are opposite hints, and OPQ and Inst FIFO are either one queue under two names or two queues. Chapter 12's 12.1-12.3 are stubs.
ssot_gap.assumed: Dispatch is by opcode; the address windows stay until the real map exists, and a write outside them is an error the model reports rather than a routing decision. One queue, one address: the port surface is the same under either chapter, which is why this does not block the boundary.

ssot_gap.desc: The tensor descriptor's scale_meta field has two meanings and no file states both, so which one applies is discoverable only by reading an implementation. isa/tensor_descriptor.toml describes it as a 'tagged pointer to scale factors for block-scaled formats; valid when dtype.scaled is set' -- the source meaning, and the only one it gives. The destination meaning is stated somewhere else entirely: isa/dfe_isa.toml's OVMM instruction overloads the *destination* descriptor's scale_meta as the Tensor Memory address of the wide (pre-narrowing) ping-pong accumulator, where ext=init zeros it before the dispatch, ext=none adds into the resident value, and a zero pointer means single-shot. Neither file says the overload is destination-only, which is the fact that makes a source unambiguous. So a reader who finds only the descriptor cannot know that an OVMM destination's pointer is not a scale tensor, and a reader who finds only the OVMM cannot know that a source's is.
ssot_gap.assumed: The operand fixes the meaning, not the field. On a source descriptor scale_meta is the companion scale tensor and only dtype.scaled makes it valid; on a destination descriptor it is the wide pre-narrowing ping-pong accumulator and never a scale pointer, because a destination receives a product that has already been scaled. The overload is destination-only, so a source is never ambiguous. Default and vanilla is dtype.scaled clear with no companion tensor -- this operand has no companion scales -- which is the configuration every path in this repo is built and tested for. That wording belongs in the descriptor's own field description and costs nothing, because the field already exists. It is recorded here instead because isa/tensor_descriptor.toml is vendored from T100_arch_spec (see UPSTREAM.toml): landing it needs an upstream change and a re-vendor, and editing the vendored copy would create exactly the two-sources-of-truth state the vendoring gate exists to prevent. fmod/src/t100_dfe/descriptor.hpp states the same rule in the same terms.

ssot_gap.desc: Where do the DFE's registers live? The architecture names the window and three registers but places none of them. Chapter 11 Table 11-2 assigns BAR0 page 1 (0x1000-0x1FFF) to 'DFE registers', and isa/dfe_isa.toml's CSRR/CSRW reg_offset is 'relative to the base of the DFE's own register window (BAR0 page 1, ch 11 11.2)'. Chapter 17 17.2 names DESC_TABLE_BASE on the DFE's register bus and chapter 4 4.2.5.4 names last_write_count and last_read_count, which chapter 11 11.3 says are never peer-writable. But chapter 17 also says 'this revision covers BAR0 page 0; remaining pages are still prose-only', and the vendored isa/t100_bar0.rdl models page 0 alone. So the DFE has a window with no offsets in it. Separately, t100.yaml places u_dfe at bar0 base 0x0C000, which is page 12, not page 1; that row predates Table 11-2 and the noc_csr tests use it as a routing fixture.
ssot_gap.assumed: ssot/regs/dfe_regs.rdl is model-only telemetry (ID, CTRL, OPS_DONE, OPS_REFUSED, ERR_STATUS) behind the noc_csr port, and it deliberately does NOT place DESC_TABLE_BASE, last_write_count or last_read_count: an invented offset for a register the architecture names becomes a software ABI the moment a host driver is written against the model, which is the failure the BAR0 page-0 mirror test exists to prevent. When the upstream SystemRDL covers page 1, vendor it through ssot/UPSTREAM.toml and mirror it the way src/hti/spec/hti_regs.rdl mirrors page 0. Until then CSRR/CSRW reaching this window is a region fault per the ISA ('an implementation may serve only its own local window, and must fault the rest'), and the t100.yaml base stays where the noc_csr fixtures expect it.

ssot_gap.desc: What does a DFE reset abandon? Chapter 4 has no reset section: it describes the instruction FIFO (4.2.2), the DFRT ready bits (4.2.3.1), the DFSC (4.2.4-4.2.5), the outstanding-completions counter (4.2.8) and the DFCQ (4.2.8.1) as steady-state structures and never says what any of them holds after rstn. Nor does it say what happens to a completion token that arrives from an engine for an entry a reset discarded, or whether the engines are reset with the DFE. Chapter 11 11.2 lists a 'reset / clocks' BAR0 page but places nothing in it, and 04-dfe-pipeline-sequence.md starts from an empty machine.
ssot_gap.assumed: A reset empties everything: the instruction FIFO, the DFRT, the DFSC, the DFCQ and the outstanding-completions counter all return to their empty initial state, last_write_count and last_read_count included, and the model's telemetry registers take their RDL reset values (csr_.reset() in onReset()). A completion token arriving after that for a cqid the reset discarded is an orphan -- counted and reported, never matched to a re-allocated entry with the same id, because that is the plausible-wrong-answer failure the unit rules exist to prevent. The engines are assumed to share the reset (one rstn from the parent), so in practice no such token arrives; the orphan path is what makes the assumption checkable rather than load-bearing.

address_map.desc: Dummy decode of the DFE's 64 KiB config window into per-engine dispatch regions.

entry.desc: Dummy window forwarded to the TDMA dispatch port.

entry.name: eu_ovmm_win
entry.desc: Dummy window forwarded to the OVMM dispatch port.

entry.name: eu_vpu_win
entry.desc: Dummy window forwarded to the VPU dispatch port.

entry.name: eu_xpu_win
entry.desc: Dummy window forwarded to the XPU dispatch port.
