fep.name: fep
fep.desc: The on-die control processor's port surface. HTI admits a region by naming its command buffer; this block walks that buffer and writes each 64-bit instruction into the DFE, then reports how the region ended. The unit QEMU cosim-direct drives with real firmware.
fep.notes: Three ports, and each one is narrower than the model used to assume. It does not see submission-queue entries -- chapter 2 2.3.2 hands it `{region_id, cmd_buf_addr, cmd_buf_bytes}` and an interrupt, and chapter 11 has HTI write the terminal CQE, so this block reports an outcome rather than completing a submission. It does not account credit either: the DFE port is AXI-Lite, and chapter 4 4.2.2 handles a full instruction FIFO by deasserting READY, so backpressure is the flow control and a bounded fifo models it unaided. What it cannot do is fetch: the command buffer lives in HBM and this boundary has no memory read (G47), which is the one gap that keeps firmware out of reach. G49 is the one place where dropping credit cost something -- a withheld handshake is not an event, so a single-threaded model has nothing to wake on and stops serving its registers while stalled.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Core clock; all three boundary interfaces are synchronous to it.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. Takes the register descriptors' reset values and abandons any region mid-walk. The command buffer survives -- it is resident in HBM and the host DMA'd it -- but the walk's position does not, because it is not architectural state.

interface.name: admit
interface.desc: Region admission in, outcome back out. This unit is the target: HTI drives the kick and this block drives the report, because it is the one that knows whether the walk finished.

interface.name: dfe
interface.desc: Instruction writes into the DFE. This unit is the AXI-Lite requester, per chapter 4 4.2.2 -- 'the FEP has an AXI Lite requester interface, through which it sends 64-bit data to DFE'. One instruction per write; the DFE withholds READY when its FIFO is full, so there is nothing to poll before pushing.

interface.name: csr
interface.desc: This unit's register window, served with RegisterFile out of the generated descriptors. Carries the enable, the region counters, and DFE_STALLS -- which is what makes a DFE-bound front end diagnosable from outside, since the stall itself is a withheld handshake and leaves no other trace. Note that the window is served between regions but not during a stall; see G49.

ssot_gap.desc: How does this block read its command buffer? Chapter 2 2.3.2 has it 'interpret the command buffer pointed to by cmd_buf_addr', which is an HBM address -- and no port on this boundary is a memory read. On hardware the front end is a CPU with its own path to memory, so the seam is presumably an AXI or fabric port that no chapter draws. Without it, no model of this unit can fetch the instructions a region names, which makes every instruction it issues fabricated rather than read.
ssot_gap.assumed: The walk stands each word in with the address it would have been fetched from, `cmd_buf_addr + i * 8`, so an ELOG replay lines up against a real program image without inventing an encoding. Nothing decodes the result. This is the gap QEMU cosim-direct closes, by making a real core do the fetch.

ssot_gap.desc: Should the DFE grant credit after all? Not for flow control -- chapter 4 4.2.2 settles that with READY -- but because a withheld handshake is not an EVENT, and that difference has a consequence the chapter does not consider. A credit update is something the writer can wait on alongside its other ports, so a front end stalled on the DFE can keep serving register reads while it waits. Backpressure gives it nothing to wait on: the fifo simply does not accept, and there is no notification when it starts accepting again. A single-threaded model therefore stops decoding CSR accesses for the whole stall, which is exactly when a host is trying to find out why it is stuck. Real hardware does not have this problem -- its register block is separate logic from its CPU -- so this is a place where the architecture is fine and a faithful model of it is not.
ssot_gap.assumed: The register plane is served between regions and not during a stall. DFE_STALLS is written before the blocking push so the count survives to be read afterwards, which recovers the diagnosis if not the liveness. Fixing it properly means two concurrent service loops in one unit, which no block in this repo does yet; the alternative is the credit counter of review proposal H7, which would make the wait selectable. Worth noting that H7 was argued from firmware convenience, and this is a second and better argument for it.

ssot_gap.desc: Is the instruction stream in the command buffer, or is the command buffer a level above it? Chapter 2 calls the resident buffer 'the region's LLIR command buffer' and chapter 8 says an interpreter on this processor 'translates the LLIR output of the compiler into the T100 instruction set'. Translating means the bytes at cmd_buf_addr are LLIR commands and the DFE instructions are produced from them -- not that the buffer holds DFE instructions to be copied. So `cmd_buf_bytes / 8` is not an instruction count, and the number of writes a region makes is not derivable from its admission at all.
ssot_gap.assumed: One instruction per 8 bytes of command buffer, which is the identity translation and is what makes the walk bounded and testable. It is wrong in the direction that matters least for the port surface -- the ports and their order are the same either way -- and right only if LLIR commands and DFE instructions happen to be one-to-one.

host_dma.name: host_dma
host_dma.desc: The HOST DMA engine: host system memory <-> HBM. Chapter 11's engine table names it `HOST`, 'host RAM <-> HBM DMA', over PCIe -- one of the four interface engines the host interface block contains, and the only one of the four whose transfer payload the architecture actually parameterises.
host_dma.notes:
Three sentences of chapter 11 fix this block's shape. 11.3.1 gives each DMA controller its own staging SRAM, so a transfer is two hops through a real buffer. 11.3 says the controller sends AXI requests to receive or transmit data to that local SRAM, so this block masters the host side through its external `host` port. 11.3.2 says a DMA completion that advances a fence is signalled only once the transferred bytes are visible in HBM to every other agent, so completion follows the HBM write response and not the last write beat.

Host DMA is not a DFE client. 4.2.8 lists the DFE completion producers as TDMA, OVMM, VPU, XPU and SEND; host DMA reports to the host-interface control logic, which produces the CQE and fence advance.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Core clock. All four interfaces are synchronous to it.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. Abandons a staged transfer without a completion, which is what t100_bar0.rdl's CTRL reset describes on the host side: 'on expiry the reset completes anyway, abandons the outstanding transfers and reports which engine and slot failed to drain'.

interface.name: xfer
interface.desc: Transfer requests in, completions back. The host interface block is the initiator and already instantiates this interface as its `dma` port, so this is the far end of an existing wire -- 11.3's 'a DMA command is pulled from HTIQ and sent to its corresponding DMA controller'. Only the flat case is executed: chapter 11 rules layout out of the transport command, so the descriptor's rank, dims and stride vectors describe something this engine does not do (interface gap G74).

interface.name: host
interface.desc: The path to host memory, and the port that replaces a back door. 11.3 has the controller 'send requests via the AXI requester interface' to move data between host memory and its local SRAM. Full AXI4 rather than Lite because a DMA hop is a burst and Lite has no AWLEN to describe one. Addresses are host IOVAs -- 11.1: 'the host-memory operand is a pinned, IOMMU-mapped IOVA' -- so 64 bits, matching the hti unit's port of the same name. Whether that is one interface shared with the hti or one per engine is G76.

interface.name: hbm
interface.desc: The device side, on all five channels. 11.3.1 puts the staging SRAM 'prior to reading or writing HBM', so this port carries the second hop of every transfer. The write direction is where 11.3.2's visibility rule bites: the completion may not be reported until this port's `b` has come back, because a completion meaning only that the controller took the bytes 'orders nothing'.

interface.name: csr
interface.desc: A telemetry window. Chapter 11's Table 11-2 reserves BAR0 page 2 for 'HOST registers' and no chapter or RDL says what they are (G75), so everything behind this port is model-only: bytes per direction, the last outcome, a sticky fault, and the counters that make this engine's refusals visible.

ssot_gap.desc: This engine has no register map. Chapter 11's Table 11-2 allocates BAR0 page 2 (0x2000-0x2FFF) to 'HOST registers' and stops; pages 3-5 are allocated the same way to NET0, DMA2 and DMA3. The SystemRDL is explicit that it does not cover them -- t100_bar0.rdl: 'Scope (current): BAR0 page 0 only ... Pages 1..15 are not yet modelled and remain prose stubs in the guide' -- and Appendix C repeats it. Chapter 17, the registers chapter, is a stub apart from DESC_TABLE_BASE. So there is an address range with a name and nothing in it.
ssot_gap.assumed: Every register behind the csr port is model-only telemetry at offsets of this unit's own choosing, and none of it configures behaviour that the transfer descriptor does not already carry. Nothing here should be read as a claim about page 2's contents. The same question was asked upstream for the execution units as T100_arch_spec#69.

ssot_gap.desc: Whose AXI requester is it? 11.3 names exactly one -- 'It contains an AXI requester interface to initiate transactions with the host, such as fetching command packets from the SQ' -- and then uses the definite article again for the DMA path: 'it sends requests via the AXI requester interface to either receive or transmit data to its local SRAM'. Read literally that is ONE port serving the SQ fetch, the CQ write, the MSI-X write and all four DMA engines' host traffic, with no arbitration described. 11.3.1 does describe a per-interface pair, but only for UCIe: 'There is an AXI responder and an AXI requester for the UCIe interface'. Nothing says whether the host engine has its own. The choice is observable: one shared requester serialises a 4 KB DMA hop against an SQ fetch, and the queue's latency then depends on DMA traffic.
ssot_gap.assumed: This unit declares its own `host` initiator, and so does the hti. Two ports, no arbitration modelled. Chosen because a unit model cannot borrow a sibling's port -- doing so would put this engine's host traffic inside the hti's model, which is precisely the coupling extracting this block was meant to undo -- and because two initiators onto one interconnect is the shape that admits either answer later: if it really is one requester, the arbiter is a thing between them, not a change to either.

ssot_gap.desc: How big is the staging SRAM, and does it bound a transfer? 11.3.1 gives every controller one -- 'Each controller has its own SRAM for staging transfers prior to reading or writing HBM' -- and gives no size, no fill/drain rule and no statement of whether a transfer larger than it is chopped into hops or refused. The HTIQ next to it is sized precisely ('8KB SRAM to hold upto 256 commands'), so the silence is specific to this buffer. It matters for more than area: a store-and-forward hop through a small buffer and a cut-through stream have different latency, different HBM burst patterns, and different answers to what 'visible in HBM' means partway through a transfer.
ssot_gap.assumed: 4096 bytes, as the stage_bytes parameter, and store-and-forward: a transfer is chopped into hops of at most that many bytes, each one read fully from the source before any of it is written to the destination. 4096 matches RFC-T100-0005 §3's 4 KB placement quantum, so a hop cannot straddle two HBM frames -- which is the one property that makes the choice more than arbitrary. Store-and-forward rather than cut-through because it is the version whose completion ordering is unambiguous, and 11.3.2 is a rule about ordering.

ssot_gap.desc: The transfer descriptor names six address spaces and chapter 11 gives this engine two. dma_interface's AddrSpace carries { tm, hbm, host, remote_hbm, nic, msic }, and this engine is anchored to { host, hbm } -- an anchor the schema has no key for, which dma_interface's own notes record. Chapter 11 agrees with the anchor by construction rather than by statement: 11.1 says 'the host-memory operand is a pinned, IOMMU-mapped IOVA and the device-memory operand is an RFC-T100-0005 tagged pointer with HBM AST', and `dir` chooses which is which. So a descriptor naming tm, msic or nic on either end is describable on the wire and undescribed by any chapter.
ssot_gap.assumed: Exactly one endpoint host and the other hbm, in either direction; anything else is refused with illegal_space and counted. This is stricter than the port and matches the chapter, and the counter is what would show a scheduler sending this engine work meant for one of the other three.

ssot_gap.desc: Which HBM stack does a device address name? The tagged pointer carries an AST nibble and a flat offset, and the hbm interface requires a stack id per request, so something has to decode one from the other -- and no chapter does. This is the same question tdma records as its G72; it recurs here because every engine touching HBM has to answer it, which is itself the argument for the decode belonging somewhere shared.
ssot_gap.assumed: Capacity-linear: 64 GiB per stack from RFC-T100-0005 §1's 384 GiB over six, so stack = offset / 64 GiB and the port gets the remainder. An offset past the populated six stacks is refused rather than aliased down into a real stack. Unlike tdma there is no window to check it against -- chapter 11 gives this engine no north/south split, and one host DMA controller reaching all of HBM is what the single AXI requester in 11.3 implies.

hti.name: hti
hti.desc: The host interface's port surface. Terminates PCIe, decodes the BAR0 aperture, fetches submission-queue packets out of host memory, admits regions to the front end, routes DMA commands to their engines, writes completions back into the host's ring, and owns the fence bank.
hti.notes: Six ports, and the two that matter most were absent from the model this replaces. Chapter 11 11.3 gives this block an AXI responder 'for initialization, reset and doorbells' and an AXI requester 'to initiate transactions with the host, such as fetching command packets from the SQ' -- so the host seam is two AXI ports, not the byte-vector PCIe record the model carried, and nothing sits between the host and this block. The requester is the port whose absence justified the model's two largest fictions: an SQ entry staged in CMD_* registers because 'no port reaches host memory', and completions published into a CQ_LAST register because nothing could write a host ring. Both are now reachable. The other four ports are unchanged in kind: a region goes to the front end, a DMA command goes to its engine, and CSR traffic goes two ways -- in from the fabric, and out to the rest of the die, which is what chapter 11 11.2 means by routing register accesses to a local and a remote register bus.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Core clock. Every interface below is synchronous to it, including the two host-facing AXI ports -- the PCIe link's own clock domain is inside the controller this block sits behind and does not reach the boundary.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. Distinct from CTRL.RESET, which is the soft reset t100_bar0.rdl describes -- that one drains outstanding transfers with a timeout and self-clears, because a host has to be able to recover a wedged card without a link retrain. This is the wire that gets there first.

interface.name: bar
interface.desc: The BAR0 aperture, as chapter 11 11.3's 'AXI responder interface for initialization, reset and doorbells'. Takes the interface's widths rather than narrowing them, which is worth saying because the aperture is narrower than both. Chapter 11 11.2 sizes BAR0 at sixteen 4KB pages, so 64KiB needs 16 address bits and the rest arrive zero -- this block still receives the whole aperture rather than only its own page, since deciding which page a request belongs to is its job and is what gives csr_egress something to carry. And 11.1.2's doorbell is 'a single 32-bit posted MMIO write', which on a 64-bit bus is a strobed half-beat rather than a narrower bus; WSTRB is what says which word, and it is the same mechanism a 64-bit fence read uses in one beat instead of two.

interface.name: host
interface.desc: The path to host memory: chapter 11 11.3's 'AXI requester interface to initiate transactions with the host, such as fetching command packets from the SQ'. Full AXI4 rather than Lite because every use of it is a burst -- a 32-byte SQ packet, a 32-byte CQE, an MSI-X write -- and Lite has no AWLEN to describe one. Addresses are host IOVAs: SQ_BASE and CQ_BASE are pinned, IOMMU-mapped, and this boundary sees them post-translation, so 64 bits. See G51 for the data width, which no chapter states.

interface.name: admit
interface.desc: Region admission out to the front end, outcome back. This unit is the initiator: chapter 2 2.3.2 has it 'hand the FEP the region's {region_id, cmd_buf_addr, cmd_buf_bytes}' and interrupt it. The report direction is this repo's contract rather than the architecture's -- see G53.

interface.name: dma
interface.desc: Descriptors out to a DMA engine, completions back. Chapter 11 11.3 has a DMA command 'pulled from HTIQ and sent to its corresponding DMA controller', and 11.3.1 has the controllers 'get their start indications from the control logic and send back completion indications' -- so this block schedules and something else moves the bytes. One port, and only the HOST engine behind it: 11.0 names four, and the other three await chapter 16 (G54).

interface.name: csr
interface.desc: This unit's registers and fence bank as reached from the die rather than from the host. Two things arrive here that the BAR cannot supply: the DFE's SIGNAL, which chapter 4 4.2.5.4 has 'send an update to the fence bank in the HTI block' and which 11.3.2 places 'on the register bus', and a PMOD or test reading this block without a host. One RegisterFile serves this port and the BAR both, so a register cannot mean two things depending on which fabric reached it.

interface.name: csr_egress
interface.desc: The remote register bus of chapter 11 11.2: 'Register accesses are routed to local register bus for registers in HTI, and to the remote register bus for registers in other parts of EIC'. Everything this block's BAR0 decode does not claim for page 0 leaves here, address unmodified. It is the port that makes BAR0 pages 1-10 reachable at all, and it is the upstream end of the CSR fabric -- which is why t100's csr_host stops being a chip-edge port once this unit is wired (G36 still blocks the far end).

ssot_gap.desc: How deep is the fence bank, and is an entry a value or a pair? Chapter 11 11.3.2 describes it twice and does not agree with itself: 'Fence registers' has a fence be a 64-bit monotonic max-merged value, while 'Fence Bank Implementation' has 512 entries each holding a pair -- `signal_cnt` and `wait_cnt` -- plus active and ready flops. Depth has three answers: t100_bar0.rdl defaults FENCE_BANK_DEPTH to 256, the implementation subsection says 512 and costs it at 512*16 = 8KB, and the sizing table gives a structural 9 + 2K for K remote streams. Separately, one wait_cnt and one active bit per entry means one registered waiter per fence, which does not obviously fit GATE_POOL.ENTRIES defaulting to 4096 pooled {fence, target} entries.
ssot_gap.assumed: The two shapes are one structure: `signal_cnt` is the fence -- the monotonic value that max-merges and that the host reads over the BAR -- and `wait_cnt` with active and ready is the gate state for a waiter registered against it, colocated because the same three-stage pipeline touches both. Implemented at 512 with one waiter slot per entry, and a second WAIT on an occupied entry is a reported error rather than a silent overwrite, since overwriting a target is how a gate opens on data that never arrived. Filed as T100_arch_spec#67.

ssot_gap.desc: How wide is the host AXI requester? Chapter 11 gives this block an AXI requester and never sizes it. The width is not free: it sets how many beats a 32-byte SQ packet or CQE costs, which is a term in 11.1.6's command round-trip floor -- the one table that budgets this path.
ssot_gap.assumed: 64 bits, so a 32-byte packet is a four-beat burst. Chosen because it is the granule everything else on this boundary already uses and needs no further justification, not because a chapter implies it. A 256-bit bus would make a packet one beat and is equally consistent with every statement in chapter 11; nothing in the model depends on which, since the burst is described by AWLEN either way.

ssot_gap.desc: Where does the MSI-X write go? Chapter 11 11.1.2 step 6 has this block 'raise the MSI-X vector assigned to the SQ/CQ pair', and 11.1.5 makes it concrete as one of 'two independent posted writes' alongside the completion data -- so it is traffic on the host requester rather than a separate interrupt port, which is why no port here carries it. But an MSI-X write needs a message address and a message data value, and those live in a PCIe capability structure that t100_bar0.rdl does not model and no chapter locates.
ssot_gap.assumed: The vector is raised as a posted write on the `host` port to an address held in a register this unit owns, defaulted to zero and therefore suppressed until a host programs it. Interface version 1.0 has one SQ/CQ pair and uses vector 0 (11.1.2), so one address and one data value is the whole table. A host that never programs it still works by polling the CQE phase bit, which 11.1 offers as the alternative.

ssot_gap.desc: How does the front end tell this block a region ended? Chapter 2 2.3.2 has HTI post the terminal KICK CQE when a region completes or faults, so this block must learn the outcome -- and no chapter describes the wire. Chapter 12 would be where it lives and is a stub. The admission direction is specified in detail; the return direction is specified only by the fact that something downstream of it happens.
ssot_gap.assumed: region_admit's `report` channel: the region_id back with a RegionStatus, driven by the front end because it is the side that knows. That makes the seam symmetric and is the smallest thing that lets the CQE be written, but it is this repo's invention and a real design might use an interrupt plus a status register, which would put the poll on this block instead.

ssot_gap.desc: Where do the other three DMA engines attach? Chapter 11 11.0 names four interface engines -- HOST, NET0, DMA2, DMA3 -- and 11.3 has this block route each DMA command to 'its corresponding DMA controller'. Only HOST has a described path (host RAM to HBM over PCIe); the other three are RoCE and peer links whose fabric is chapter 16, which is a one-line stub. So the routing exists in the architecture and the destinations do not.
ssot_gap.assumed: One `dma` port, reaching the HOST engine. A command naming another engine is a reported error rather than a fourth port left dangling, because three unconnected ports would each need a peer that has no spec, and an error says the same thing more usefully.

ssot_gap.desc: What is BAR1 for, in detail? Chapter 11 11.2 names it once -- 'the BAR1 aperture is used for DMA transfers with the host' -- with no size, no map, and no statement of how it relates to the SQ/CQ rings, which live in host memory reached over the requester rather than in an aperture. A host-visible aperture the device DMAs through is a different mechanism from a device-pull fetch, and the chapter uses both without distinguishing them.
ssot_gap.assumed: Not modelled. This boundary carries BAR0 only, and the `bar` port's 16 address bits say so. Every path chapter 11 describes end to end -- doorbell, SQ fetch, CQE write, MSI-X -- is reachable without BAR1, so leaving it out costs nothing that is currently specified.

ssot_gap.desc: Where does the fence bank live in the BAR map? Chapter 11 11.3.2 sizes it at 512 entries of two 64-bit counters and says it can be SRAM with a single port -- an 8KB aperture, not a flop CSR file, and not something a 4KB page (Table 11-2) holds without four rows per fence. t100_bar0.rdl publishes FENCE_CAP but does not place the bank.
ssot_gap.assumed: A separate BAR window whose base is invented by this model, with depth published in FENCE_CAP. Filed as T100_arch_spec#67.

noc_csr.name: noc_csr
noc_csr.desc: The T100 CSR fabric: transport for chip-wide control-register access. Two initiators (the host path via HIB, and the SMP) are arbitrated onto one fabric egress; an address inside this block's own BAR0 window terminates locally. Single outstanding access, strict ordering -- the contract is functionally an APB fabric, and APB is PREADY-gated one at a time.
noc_csr.notes: The local claim is behavior, not an address map: this block's window has no register map yet, so unmapped-in-window is an error like any other unit's hole. It appears below as bar0_base / bar0_span parameters rather than an [[unit.address_map]] entry, because an address_map entry can only be a `forward` onto another local interface and a local claim is not a forward. The egress is one port, not one port per target, so chip-wide routing is not expressible on this surface -- do not add a decoder for everyone else's windows here.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: CSR fabric clock; all three boundary interfaces are synchronous to it.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset.

interface.name: smp
interface.desc: CSR requests from the system-management processor. Arbitrated ahead of the host path, so management access never waits behind an unbounded host stream.

interface.name: ingress
interface.desc: CSR requests arriving from the host path (BAR writes through the HIB). This block is the target.

interface.name: egress
interface.desc: The single fabric egress: every address not claimed locally leaves here, absolute and unmodified. Not one port per target.

pcr.name: pcr
pcr.desc: Owns the chip's clock and reset domains. The boot sequence controller commands a domain's clock and reset state; this block latches it, reports back what it holds, and refuses a transition that would release a domain before its clock runs.
pcr.notes: The refusal is the interesting half. A command that deasserts reset while the clock is gated is a sequencing bug rather than a request to serve: the status channel echoes the unchanged latch and the model asserts, on the grounds that a boot sequencer issuing an illegal transition should be caught in simulation and not tolerated at runtime. Four domains, not the chip map -- the count comes from the register file, which is the only place that names them (pcr gap G31). Software sees the applied state through read-only DOMAIN<n> registers, so a driver can observe the boot walk without being able to drive it.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: The always-on domain's clock. This block cannot take its clock from a domain it gates, so it runs on the one domain it is not allowed to turn off.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. Takes the register descriptors' reset values, which hold every domain clock-gated and in reset -- the only safe power-on state, since a domain that came up released would run before its clock was characterized.

interface.name: domain
interface.desc: The domain-control port. This block is the target: it receives commands and drives the status channel, because it is the one that knows what state a domain actually reached.

interface.name: csr
interface.desc: This unit's register window, served with RegisterFile out of the generated descriptors. Every register is read-only to software: the domains are hardware-written when a command applies, so a driver can watch the boot walk without being able to drive it out from under the sequencer.

ssot_gap.desc: Which unit is the initiator on the domain port? The manifest names `boot_seq`, in a boot protocol of `RoT -> boot sequence controller -> per-block release`. But boot_seq is registered at flavors: [unspecified] -- the block is on the diagram and nothing is behind it -- so nothing owns the other end. It is also unstated whether that controller is a distinct block or a mode of the RoT, which decides whether this port crosses a unit boundary at all.
ssot_gap.assumed: The initiator is a testbench. src/pcr/cosim_test drives the port directly, and t100_unit.toml declares no connection for it, so the port is unconnected in the assembly rather than wired to a stand-in -- a stand-in would fix a topology nothing has chosen.

send.name: send
send.desc: The SEND engine: moves a tile out of tensor memory to the interface its instruction names -- tensor memory again, or one of the two MS memory buffers on the MSIC. The fifth of the DFE's dispatch targets, and the die's only path to the metasurface.
send.notes:
4.2.6 steers the issue stage's pick mux into one of five FIFOs -- 'TDMA instruction FIFO, OVMM instruction FIFO, VPU instruction FIFO, XPU instruction FIFO, SEND instruction FIFO' -- and 4.2.8 lists the same five units as completion-token producers. This unit terminates the DFE's `ucie` port for SEND and TSEND.

Chapter 5 is the worked example this block has to make work: 'SEND instruction sends 2 weight tiles to the MSIC to meta surface memory buffer A', then MSLOADA, then OVMM with msync. Two SENDs to one buffer before one load is what forces the buffer to be addressed rather than filled from zero (ms_buf G81).

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Core clock. All five interfaces are synchronous to it.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. Abandons a transfer in flight without a completion token, which wedges the DFCQ head -- the same exposure every dispatch target has, and the reason a reset is a whole-region event rather than a per-unit one.

interface.name: dfe
interface.desc: Dispatch in: opcode, the resolved source descriptor, the 5-bit dst_type selector, and the cqid and source id to quote back. Named for the peer rather than the interface type, because a port called `ucie` says less about what crosses it than the DFE does. This is the far end of a wire that existed -- dfe_unit.toml has declared this port and dfe_fmod has pushed SEND and TSEND onto it with no consumer.

interface.name: cmp
interface.desc: The completion token back, one per dispatch. 4.2.8 names SEND as one of the five units that return one. Target role even though the payload flows outward -- the interface fixes the DFE as initiator. Its dst field is always invalid here, which is ucie G84: 4.2.3 says a SEND's completion info contains a destination descriptor, but chapter 3 gives SEND and TSEND no dst field to read and the address format has no code for MSIC SRAM, so the model clears it and asks upstream (T100_arch_spec#70) rather than inventing a ready bit.

interface.name: tm
interface.desc: Tensor memory, on all five channels. Always the source -- 4.2.5.2 has SEND move data 'from TM' -- and sometimes also the destination, because dst_type's 0b00000 is tensor memory, which makes a SEND to it a TM-to-TM copy and a TSEND to it a TM-to-TM transpose.

interface.name: ms
interface.desc: The MS memory buffers on the MSIC, write-only. The destination for dst_type 0b00001 and 0b00010. This interface is new and derived from two table rows -- see its own G80 for how little the architecture says about what is on the other side.

interface.name: csr
interface.desc: A telemetry window. No chapter gives this engine a register map (G88), so everything behind this port is model-only: bytes per destination, the transpose count, the last outcome and a sticky fault.

ssot_gap.desc: Does T100 support an MSIC-to-TM read path or strided SEND transfers? The ISA defines SEND/TSEND from TM toward an MS buffer, carries no explicit length, and names no instruction that reads an MS buffer back into TM.
ssot_gap.assumed: SEND is one-way from TM to the selected MS buffer. No reverse or independently strided transfer is modeled until the architecture names an instruction and boundary for it.

ssot_gap.desc: This engine has no register map. Chapter 11's Table 11-2 allocates BAR0 pages to the DFE and the four host-interface engines and nothing to this one; the SystemRDL covers page 0 only and says so; chapter 17 is a stub apart from DESC_TABLE_BASE. The same question was asked upstream for the execution units as T100_arch_spec#69, and this unit inherits it.
ssot_gap.assumed: Every register behind the csr port is model-only telemetry at offsets of this unit's own choosing, and none of it configures behaviour the dispatch does not already carry. A completion token has no status field (completion G16), so a refusal has nowhere else to be reported.

ssot_gap.desc: Can a SEND be in flight while another is dispatched? Nothing states it. 4.2.6 gives this engine an instruction FIFO, which implies queuing ahead of it rather than concurrency inside it, and 4.2.8.1 retires the DFCQ in order regardless. What makes the question sharper here than for the TDMA is chapter 5's example: two SENDs fill buffer A before one MSLOADA reads it, so the second SEND's ordering against the first is load-bearing for correctness and not only for throughput.
ssot_gap.assumed: Strictly one at a time -- the next dispatch is not read until the current one's token has gone back. The slowest correct behaviour, and the only one that cannot produce an ordering no chapter has blessed. It also makes chapter 5's two-tile sequence deterministic, which a concurrent engine would not.

ssot_gap.desc: A TSEND to tensor memory is a transpose that does not involve the MSIC at all, and the XPU is described as the transpose unit with its own dispatch port. So two blocks transpose tiles in TM, reached by two different instructions on two different ports, and nothing says which a compiler should emit or whether the results are required to agree bit for bit.
ssot_gap.assumed: Both exist and both do what their own chapters say. This unit implements TSEND by swapping the tile's two extents, which is the XPU's reading of the same operation (xpu G62), so the two at least agree. Not treated as blocking because a send that transposes is expressible either way; the overlap is a question about the ISA's shape, not about this boundary.

smp.name: smp
smp.desc: The T100 system management processor's port surface: a CSR target on its own BAR0 window, and a CSR initiator into the fabric. On the hardware this is a RISC-V core doing housekeeping -- redundancy, calibration loops, telemetry -- and it reaches every other block as the second initiator on the Arteris CSR fabric, never through the datapath.
smp.notes: The model is not that core. It is the two things the rest of the chip can already observe: a register window served out of spec/smp_regs.rdl, and a programmable stub that turns a doorbell write into a canned calibration write sequence with single-outstanding tag correlation. Which is why this unit has a register surface at all -- a real core would hold the target address and payload in its own memory, and the stub takes them from CAL_ADDR / CAL_DATA / CAL_SEQ. Both interfaces below carry the same type: this unit is a target on one and an initiator on the other, which is the whole of its CSR-path role.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: CSR clock; both boundary interfaces are synchronous to it.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. Takes the register descriptors' reset values and leaves no outstanding management access behind.

interface.name: csr
interface.desc: This unit's own BAR0 window. Served with RegisterFile out of the generated descriptors, so swaccess rules and the doorbell come from the register spec rather than being re-derived here.

interface.name: csr_init
interface.desc: Management accesses this unit issues, as the fabric's second initiator. Absolute addresses, deliberately not range-checked here: deciding which unit an address belongs to is the fabric's job, and a decode miss returns as an error the model latches.

ssot_gap.desc: How many management accesses may be outstanding at once? The model issues one, because the contract it initiates into is 'functionally an APB fabric' and APB is PREADY-gated one at a time. Nothing states whether the real core is allowed to pipeline, and a core that could would need tag correlation deeper than one entry.
ssot_gap.assumed: Single outstanding. A response whose tag does not match the one request in flight is counted as a downstream protocol violation and dropped, rather than retiring the outstanding access.

t100.name: t100
t100.desc: T100 EIC assembly: the config-built unit tree. Holds the CSR fabric, SMP, PCR, FEP, HTI, the DFE, and the four DFE engines that are subunits today (XPU, north TDMA, SEND, host DMA). The DFE's dispatch and completion ports now have peers in this tree for three of the five engines, declared below and -- like every other connection here -- not yet auto-wired (#245). Exposes the host-side CSR port at the chip edge for a test harness to drive.
t100.notes: The shape this file proves is spec -> generated config -> libyy auto-build -> typed ports carrying generated bundles. Being in subunits[] and being connected are separate things, and u_pcr is the first unit where they come apart: it is built from config like the others, but the fabric has one egress and u_smp has it (G36). The remaining three CSR-path units will arrive the same way, so G36 is what gates the assembly becoming a wired chip rather than a construction proof. u_hti and u_fep are the first pair whose datapath connection is between two real subunits rather than a subunit and a stand-in. csr_host stays external by design -- per Phase 8's F9, wiring a chip-edge port is the application's business, so the harness connects it and nothing in the config tries to.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Chip clock; the CSR fabric runs synchronous to it.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Chip reset, synchronous and active-low.

subunit.desc: The Arteris low-speed NoC: the CSR fabric.
The system management processor: a CSR target on its own window, and the fabric's second initiator.

Power / clock / reset: owns the clock and reset domains. Present so it is built from config like the others; neither of its ports is connected here, for two different reasons -- see G36 and pcr's G35.

The front-end processor: walks a region's command buffer and writes instructions into the DFE. Its admit port has a peer -- u_hti, below -- and so does its dfe port now that u_dfe is in the tree; its CSR port still has nowhere to go (G36).

The dataflow engine, the dispatch hub every engine below is downstream of. Its cfg_axi ingress is the far end of u_fep's dfe port; its tdma, eu_xpu and ucie dispatch ports and its cmp completion port have peers in u_tdma_n, u_xpu and u_send. All of that is declared in [[unit.connection]] and none of it is auto-wired (#245), so it is built from config and arrives unwired like the rest. eu_ovmm and eu_vpu have no peer: the OVMM and VPU are not subunits here. Its csr port is model-only telemetry with nowhere to go (G36, and dfe's G95).

The transpose engine. Its eu and cmp ports face u_dfe, which is in this assembly now and named as their peer in [[unit.connection]]; its tm port faces tensor memory, which is not a unit at all. Declared is not wired (#245), so it is still built from config and left entirely unwired.

The north tensor DMA engine, reaching HBM stacks 0-2. Unwired for the same reasons u_xpu is: its dispatch and completion ports have u_dfe as their declared peer but nothing wires a declaration (#245), and both memory ports face things that are not units at all. Its SOUTH twin is deliberately absent -- see the parameter-override gap below, which this unit is the first to hit.

The SEND engine, tensor memory out to the MS memory buffers on the MSIC. Unwired because its dispatch and completion ports are only declared against u_dfe (#245), tensor memory is not a unit, and its `ms` port faces the MSIC on a different die.

The HOST DMA engine, host system memory <-> HBM. Its `xfer` port is the far end of u_hti's `dma` port, so unlike u_xpu and u_tdma_n this one has a peer in this assembly -- but the wiring is still absent for the same reason theirs is, and there is a second reason here: the `host` port is external by construction, since host memory is on the other side of PCIe.

The host interface: terminates PCIe, fetches the submission queue out of host memory, admits regions to u_fep and posts completions back. The first subunit whose external ports are the chip's host edge rather than a stand-in.

interface.name: csr_host
interface.desc: Chip-edge CSR initiator standing in for the host path (HIB BAR writes) until the HIB joins the assembly.

connection.desc: The SMP as the fabric's second initiator: management accesses, arbitrated ahead of the host path so they never wait behind an unbounded host stream.

The region execution seam: ch2 2.3.2 and ch11 11.1.2 have the host interface hand the front end a region tuple and an interrupt, not the raw queue entry. The first connection here between two subunits that both have models.

SQ DMA opcode to the host DMA engine. Both ends are in this tree -- u_host_dma.xfer is the far end of u_hti's dma port -- and like u_hti.admit this is declared rather than auto-wired (#245). The host port stays unwired regardless: host memory is on the other side of PCIe.
The instruction ingress, ch4 4.2.2: the FEP's AXI-Lite requester into the DFE's responder, one 64-bit store per instruction. READY-deassert is the whole flow control (dfe's G42).
Dispatch to the north TDMA, ch4 4.2.6. The south engine would take the same port and is absent for the reason G73 gives.
Dispatch to the XPU, ch4 4.2.6. The eu_ovmm and eu_vpu siblings have no peer here: OVMM and VPU are not subunits.
Completion tokens back to the DFE, ch4 4.2.8. Three engines fan in onto one DFE port; the arbitration is parent wiring policy, which is exactly what is not written down yet (#245).
XPU completion to the DFE, ch4 4.2.8; fan-in as above.
SEND completion to the DFE, ch4 4.2.8; fan-in as above.
The fabric egress into the SMP's own BAR0 window. One port, matching the egress: this is not a chip-wide decode, and it is why only one downstream target is expressible here today.

ssot_gap.desc: How does the CSR fabric reach more than one downstream target? `noc_csr` has a single `egress` interface -- every address it does not claim locally leaves by that one port, absolute and unmodified -- so the assembly can name exactly one downstream CSR target, and the SMP has it. u_pcr is the first unit to arrive with nowhere to be connected, and the remaining six will each arrive the same way. Two shapes would answer it and they are not equivalent: one egress per target, which puts a window table and a decode inside the fabric, or one egress onto a shared bus that every target snoops, which puts the decode in each target. The register maps already exist in t100.yaml, so the information for either is there; nothing states which the hardware does.
ssot_gap.assumed: One target, and it is u_smp. Every other subunit's CSR port is left unconnected in the assembly rather than wired through a stand-in, because a stand-in would commit to one of the two shapes above. Unit tests drive each CSR port directly, which is what they did before the assembly existed.

ssot_gap.desc: A unit instantiated twice with different parameters cannot be expressed. The TDMA is the first: t100.yaml has u_tdma_n serving HBM stacks 0-2 and u_tdma_s serving 3-5, which tdma_unit.toml carries as stack_first / stack_count, and the model range-checks every dispatch against them. But `parameters` belong to a UNIT, not to an instance -- unit_schema.toml's [unit.subunit] admits only instance, unit, desc and count, and libyy's Subunit struct matches it -- so two instances of `tdma` necessarily share one window. Writing both here would silently make the south engine a second north one, which is worse than omitting it: every dispatch aimed at stacks 3-5 would be refused as bad_stack by a block whose name says it should have accepted them. Note this is not specific to the TDMA; the nine PCIe ports and the six HBM controllers will each want it.
ssot_gap.assumed: u_tdma_n only, and the south instance omitted until a per-instance parameter override exists. The unit model itself is complete and parameterised, so nothing about the block is waiting on this -- the gap is in the assembly's expressiveness, and it is tracked as models#255.

tdma.name: tdma
tdma.desc: The tensor DMA engine. Chapter 4 Table 4.2.5.2: 'Tiled HBM read or write to the tensor memory DMA unit. Contiguous transfers move data HBM to TM (reads) and TM to HBM (writes); strided transfers move tiles to and from TM. MZERO writes zero data to HBM.' Two instances on the die, north and south, differing only in which HBM stacks they reach.
tdma.notes:
4.2.6 gives TDMA its own instruction FIFO off the DFE pick mux, represented by the `tdma` interface. The DFE resolves tensor descriptors before dispatch; TDMA returns the architectural completion token and has no separate SIGNAL output because SIGNAL is a DFE opcode.

The load-bearing rule is 4.2.8: 'Retirement of a write means the data is globally visible.' A TDMA completion for MWRITE, MSTWRITE, MZERO, or DSTORE is returned only after the HBM port's write response, never merely after the last data beat.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Core clock. All five interfaces are synchronous to it.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. Abandons a transfer in flight without a completion token, which is safe only because the DFE's tables reset alongside -- there is nothing left waiting on the result.

interface.name: dfe
interface.desc: Transfer work in. Named for the peer rather than for the interface type, because a port called `tdma` on the unit called tdma says nothing. The DFE already instantiates this interface as its `tdma` port, so this is the far end of an existing wire: opcode, the cqid and descriptor ids to quote back, two resolved descriptors, and the HBM address DLOAD/DSTORE name.

interface.name: cmp
interface.desc: The completion token back, one per dispatch. Target role even though the payload flows outward -- the interface fixes the DFE as initiator. For a write instruction this port is where 4.2.8's visibility rule is observable: the token must not appear until the hbm port's `b` has.

interface.name: hbm
interface.desc: The HBM side of every transfer, on all five channels. This unit is the initiator: MREAD reads here, MWRITE and MZERO write here, DSTORE writes a descriptor here. The `stack` field is range-checked against this instance's stack_first/stack_count, which is what makes north and south different blocks rather than one block with a comment.

interface.name: tm
interface.desc: The tensor-memory side, also five channels and also as initiator. MREAD writes here and MWRITE reads here, so unlike the hbm port this one is not touched at all by MZERO or the descriptor-move instructions.

interface.name: csr
interface.desc: A telemetry window, and nothing architectural. Every register behind it is model-only for the same reason the XPU's are (xpu G59, asked as T100_arch_spec#69): no chapter and no upstream RDL describes this unit's registers. What it holds is what the completion token cannot -- bytes moved per direction, the last outcome, a sticky fault -- plus the counters that make this unit's refusals visible.

ssot_gap.desc: Chapter 21 is a stub. 'Tensor DMA Unit' followed by five empty section headings, so the unit's own normative chapter says nothing about its geometry, its ordering, its error behaviour or its register interface. Everything this block does is assembled from chapter 4, which describes the TDMA from the DFE's side: which opcodes reach it, that its write completions mean global visibility, and that it is one of the five units returning completion tokens. That is enough to build a transfer engine and not enough to know whether this one matches the intended hardware.
ssot_gap.assumed: Chapter 4 is treated as normative for everything it covers, and anything it does not cover is refused rather than invented. In practice that means one contiguous transfer per dispatch, bounded by what the two memory ports can express, with every unhandled case counted in a register.

ssot_gap.desc: How long is a transfer? Neither the instruction nor the descriptor states a byte count. The dispatch carries two resolved descriptors and the descriptor carries extents -- `dims` per tensor and `tdims` per tile -- but no field says which of them bounds THIS transfer, and the source and destination descriptors can disagree about all of them. For MZERO there is only one descriptor and no source to agree with. The hbm and tm ports both take `len` in bytes, so a number has to be produced from somewhere.
ssot_gap.assumed: The transfer length is the source's tile: tdims[0] x tdims[1] x element bytes, matching the XPU's reading of the same fields (xpu G63), and for MZERO the destination's tile instead. The destination's extents are then CHECKED against it rather than trusted -- a dispatch whose two descriptors describe different-sized tiles is refused, because moving the smaller count would silently truncate and moving the larger would overrun a buffer the compiler sized.

ssot_gap.desc: Nothing checks that a descriptor's memory matches the direction the opcode implies. MREAD moves HBM to TM, so its source should be an HBM-tagged pointer and its destination a UTM-tagged one; MWRITE the reverse. The descriptor's AST nibble states which space it is in, and the opcode states the direction, so the two can contradict each other -- and no chapter says which wins, or that the case is illegal. 4.2.9's illegal-opcode list is close but not this: it gives 'instruction uses the wrong type of descriptor. For instance, an MREAD from a tensor descriptor to another tensor descriptor is not supported as it requires an HBM to HBM transfer', which names the case and calls it unsupported without saying what the unit does about it.
ssot_gap.assumed: The AST nibbles must agree with the opcode's direction, and a dispatch where they do not is refused and counted. 4.2.9 says the DCHK block in the DFE performs this check, so a refusal here should be unreachable in a correct system -- which is exactly why it is worth counting rather than asserting: a nonzero count means DCHK is not doing it.

ssot_gap.desc: The descriptor names an HBM byte and the port wants a stack, and nothing connects the two. A tagged pointer's HBM form is a flat 42-bit offset (isa/tensor_descriptor.toml: 'HBM byte offset; 4 TiB virtual envelope') with no stack field. The hbm port requires one and is explicit that it will not help: 'The initiator names it; this port never derives it from the address', and its own gap G26 leaves where the id comes from 'to the initiator, so no policy is compiled in here'. This unit IS that initiator, so the policy has to be compiled in HERE, and no chapter states it. RFC-T100-0005 §3 makes the situation worse rather than better: it says placement is the allocator's, carried per 4 KB frame in a PTE as `stack[2:0]` and `side`, and that there is deliberately no arithmetic decode at access time -- but a resolved descriptor carries no PTE, so the one mechanism the architecture describes is not reachable from this port.
ssot_gap.assumed: Capacity-linear: a stack holds 64 GiB (RFC-T100-0005 §1, 384 GiB across six), so stack = addr >> 36 and the stack-local address is the low 36 bits. This is arithmetic the RFC explicitly says the hardware does not do, and it is chosen anyway because it is checkable -- an address past the populated 384 GiB decodes to a stack id of 6 or more and is refused rather than aliased, and a transfer whose span would cross a stack boundary is refused too. A guessed interleave would instead scatter bytes at plausible addresses on the wrong stack. The correct fix is upstream of this unit: either the DFE resolves placement when it resolves the descriptor, or the descriptor grows a stack field.

ssot_gap.desc: One transfer, two memories, and no statement of how much may be in flight. The visibility rule in 4.2.8 constrains when a write's token may be returned but says nothing about whether this engine may have several transfers open at once, or whether a later transfer's reads may pass an earlier one's writes. Both memory ports are tagged and both document per-tag ordering only, so the ports permit reordering that the architecture never discusses. Two instances make it sharper: nothing says whether north and south may reorder against each other.
ssot_gap.assumed: One transfer at a time, start to finish, with the completion token issued before the next dispatch is accepted. This is the slowest correct behaviour and the only one that cannot produce an ordering the architecture has not blessed. It is also visibly a placeholder: a real engine would pipeline, and doing so is the first thing that needs an answer here.

xpu.name: xpu
xpu.desc: The transpose engine. Chapter 22: 'the engine that performs transpose operations on data tiles. The dataflow engine (DFE) issues XPU work from transpose-class instructions in the T100 ISA'. One tile in from tensor memory, its transpose back out, and a completion token to the DFE.
xpu.notes: Four ports, and the deletions are the point. There is no engine-command bus: 4.2.6 gives this unit its own instruction FIFO off the DFE's pick mux, so the FIFO is the addressing and nothing on the wire names the engine -- which is what the `eu` interface, already owned by the DFE and already carrying resolved descriptors, is. There is no signal output: SIGNAL is a DFE opcode (4.2.5.4) and 4.2.8 says completion tokens are 'DFE-internal', so an engine has no fence path at all. And there are no geometry registers: 4.2.5 has the issue stage resolve the descriptor and send 'base address, dimensions and data type ... as part of the instruction', so the extents arrive with the work rather than being programmed ahead of it. See models#252 for the seam and T100_arch_spec#68 for what chapter 22 leaves blank -- which is most of it.

clock.name: clk
clock.desc: Core clock. All three interfaces are synchronous to it; the credit-based interconnect that 4.2.6 puts between the DFE and this unit is inside the fabric and does not reach the boundary.

reset.name: rstn
reset.desc: Synchronous, active-low reset. Abandons a transpose in flight without a completion token, which is safe only because the DFE's ready table resets alongside -- there is nothing left waiting on the result.

interface.name: eu
interface.desc: Transpose work in. The DFE already owns this interface and already instantiates it three times -- eu_ovmm, eu_vpu, eu_xpu -- so this is the far end of a wire that exists, not a new one. It carries the opcode and three RESOLVED 64-byte tensor descriptors, which is where the tile's base address, extents and data type come from; vpu_kernel_addr is not this unit's and is ignored. Target role: the DFE drives cmd and valid, this block drives ready.

interface.name: cmp
interface.desc: The completion token back, one per dispatch, exactly chapter 4's 27-bit `completion_token`: dst sets a DFRT Rdy bit and src0 releases its RdCnt. Target role even though the payload flows outward -- the interface fixes initiator as the DFE, so this block drives payload and valid and the DFE drives ready. src1 is never valid here: a transpose has one source.

interface.name: tm
interface.desc: The tile in and the transpose out. This unit is the initiator on all five channels: it reads the source tile as a burst, permutes it internally, and writes the result as a burst. Both endpoints are tensor-memory offsets the dispatch resolved, so this block computes no address of its own beyond decoding an offset into the port's (bank, offset) pair -- which is the decode tm gap G11 says is probably wrong.

interface.name: csr
interface.desc: A telemetry window, and nothing architectural. Every register behind it is model-only: the architecture defines no XPU registers at all (G59), and the geometry registers this block used to carry were standing in for descriptor resolution that 4.2.5 specifies happens in the DFE. What is left is what makes a dispatched engine diagnosable from outside -- operations completed, last outcome, sticky fault -- which is the one thing the completion token cannot carry (completion gap G16: no status field, so a refused dispatch and a successful one are indistinguishable on the wire).

ssot_gap.desc: Does this unit have a register window at all? The architecture defines no XPU registers. Chapter 22 is four empty headings, no SystemRDL file describes the unit, and chapter 17 17.2 names exactly one register on the DFE's register bus (DESC_TABLE_BASE), which is not this block's. But the architecture does imply a register plane reaching blocks: chapter 11 Table 11-2 sizes BAR0 at sixteen pages and the systemrdl README says pages 1-15 -- 'DFE, interface engines, reset/clocks, configuration, power management, performance counters, telemetry, reserved' -- 'are not yet modelled and remain prose stubs'. Performance counters and telemetry are named page purposes, so something is meant to be there. Nothing says what, or which page a compute engine falls under; Table 11-2's wording is 'interface engines', and a transpose unit is not one.
ssot_gap.assumed: A model-only window, marked as such in the RDL, holding what a diagnostic needs and nothing that pretends to be architectural: an operation count, the last outcome, and a sticky fault bit. It is deliberately NOT a mirror of anything, unlike hti's map, because there is no upstream map to mirror. Asked as T100_arch_spec#69, which is worth answering once rather than per engine -- every remaining compute and DMA unit raises it identically.

ssot_gap.desc: Is a transpose in-place, and how large a tile may it be? Nothing says. If src0 == dst is legal this unit needs a whole tile of internal buffering; if it is not, something should reject the aliased case and nothing specifies what. The size question compounds it: 2.5.1 has tile size 'chosen by the compiler' and varying 'from a few elements to the whole tensor', so an in-place requirement would put an unbounded buffer inside the block. Chapter 22 22.2's heading promises 'Row-major / column-major and other supported tensor layouts' and has no body, and the descriptor's layout field points at chapter 6's DSFC section, which is also a stub -- so the set of layout transforms this unit performs is undefined even before the geometry is.
ssot_gap.assumed: Out-of-place, and a tile that fits one tensor-memory bank. Out-of-place because an unbounded internal buffer is not a thing to model by accident; bank-sized because the tm port cannot express a burst crossing a bank (tm gap G24) and so a larger tile would have to be split, which is a datapath this block does not have. A dispatch naming a larger tile, or naming the same address for source and destination, is refused and recorded rather than attempted.

ssot_gap.desc: The element type cannot be decoded, and it is not clear which types this unit implements. Two separate problems in one 8-bit field. (1) THE WIDTH ENCODING IS NOT DEFINED. isa/tensor_descriptor.toml describes dtype.width as 'Element width: log2 bits or a sub-byte code' over the formats FP4, FP6, FP8, BF16, FP16, FP32, INT4, INT8, and refers to '5.1' for the detail -- but chapter 5 is the OVMM chapter and defines no such encoding. 'log2 bits or a sub-byte code' is two encodings sharing four bits with no discriminator, so nothing turns a dtype into a byte count, which is the one thing a transpose needs from it. (2) WHICH TYPES DOES THIS UNIT SUPPORT? Table 2.2 is introduced as 'the data types that will be supported by the OVMM, VPU and XPU' -- one table for three units, which does not say each supports all of it. The list includes the block-scaled MXFP formats, whose scale_meta companion tensor a transpose would have to permute alongside the data or silently corrupt, and the descriptor carries a `scaled` bit this unit therefore does not know what to do with.
ssot_gap.assumed: width is read as log2 of the element's bit count, and only values that yield a whole number of bytes are accepted: 3, 4, 5 and 6 for 1, 2, 4 and 8 bytes. Sub-byte widths are refused rather than guessed at -- FP4 and INT4 pack two elements per byte, so permuting them needs bit-level addressing that neither this block nor the tm port can express, and a wrong guess produces plausible-looking wrong data rather than an error. A dtype with the scaled bit set is likewise refused, because permuting the data and leaving its scale tensor behind is the worst available outcome. Everything accepted is permuted as opaque bytes, which is correct for any unscaled format: a transpose moves elements without interpreting them.

ssot_gap.desc: Which descriptor is the source and which is the destination, and is src1 ever used? The eu interface names three operand slots because OVMM needs three (two sources and a result), and one interface serves OVMM, VPU and XPU. Chapter 22 is four empty headings and never says how a transpose fills them. A transpose is one-in one-out, so one slot must go unused, and nothing states which. The completion token has the same shape and the same silence.
ssot_gap.assumed: src0 is the tile to read, dst is where the transpose is written, src1 is unused and its descriptor is ignored. This is the only assignment consistent with the DFE model, which fills src0 from the instruction's src0 field and dst from its dst field for every group alike, and with the DFRT semantics -- dst sets a Rdy bit, so the slot that sets Rdy has to be the one written. A dispatch arriving with a non-zero src1 descriptor is not an error and is not read; it is counted, because a non-zero src1 would mean this reading is wrong. Part of T100_arch_spec#68.

ssot_gap.desc: The tile geometry has two candidate sources in one descriptor and the choice changes what a transpose means. tensor_descriptor.toml carries both `dims` (4 x 32-bit, 'logical extent per tensor dimension in elements') and `tdims` (4 x 32-bit, 'logical extent per tile dimension'), and 2.5.1 has a tensor covered by an array of tiles whose size the compiler chooses. Chapter 22 says this unit 'performs transpose operations on data tiles', so tdims looks right -- but nothing says whether one dispatch transposes one tile or walks the whole tile array, and if it walks, nothing gives the array's stride. Chapter 6's DSFC layout section, which the descriptor's `layout` field points at for how tiles are placed in memory, is a stub.
ssot_gap.assumed: One dispatch is one tile: tdims[0] x tdims[1] elements read from base, written transposed to the destination's base, with dims and layout ignored. Chapter 22's own wording is 'on data tiles', and this is the reading that needs no stride the spec does not define. A dispatch whose tdims are zero, or whose tile does not fit a tensor-memory bank (G60), is refused rather than clipped.

ssot_gap.desc: The DFE cannot currently drive this port. eu gap G13 records the open question -- resolved descriptors or descriptor indices -- and the DFE model has already answered it the other way: dfe_fmod fills each 64-byte slot with the raw unresolved 8-bit index in its low bits, because DFDT resolution does not exist in the model yet. So u_dfe and u_xpu agree on the wire's shape and disagree on its contents, and a descriptor arriving from the DFE today decodes to base 0, dtype 0, tdims 0 -- which this unit refuses as a zero extent.
ssot_gap.assumed: This unit implements the interface as specified, i.e. resolved. The refusal path makes the disagreement loud rather than silent: an index-filled descriptor is rejected and counted in ERR_STATUS instead of transposing zero bytes and returning a successful token. The two are connected in the assembly but the pairing does not do useful work until the DFE resolves descriptors, which is G13's blocking half.
